articles.title: What the US and China Should Discuss at APEC
articles.full_text:
Both sides are feeding an AI investment bubble – and Shenzhen is the place to talk about it.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump shake hands during their summit at the White House, Sep. 24, 2026.
On September 24, the presidents of the United States and China met in Washington and agreed to build what their joint language calls a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” On November 18-19, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet again, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. Two summits in three months is a rare occurrence in China-U.S. relations. 
In the September summit, already their second of 2026, one key area stood out as the focus: artificial intelligence. The risks of AI now have a dedicated channel for discussion. There’s not yet a corresponding China-U.S. platform for talking about the economics of the AI race. 
During Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May, the two leaders agreed to restart government-to-government AI dialogue. In September, at the eighth round of economic consultations in New York and Washington, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held the first AI dialogue within that framework. They agreed to establish a channel for communications on AI incidents, and scheduled a second round of talks before the end of November. 
Shortly thereafter, at the presidential summit, Xi described China and the United States as two AI powers that should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other.” He added, “The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI.” Trump noted that discussions on “pressing issues” related to (among other topics) AI, which he calls “superintelligence,” could “promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come.” Both leaders thus offered the new dialogue platform political cover.
That is genuine progress, with a revealing limit. All the steps thus far – the exchanges on risks and benefits, the incident channel, the push for lab self-regulation – concern the dangers AI might create. Nothing yet addresses the looming economic problem of the AI sector. 
In the United States, recent developments are rather worrying. The business model for U.S. frontier AI businesses assumes that compute demand will keep growing exponentially, model capability will convert reliably into revenue, and capital will stay patient. All three assumptions are looking increasingly risky. 
The capex needed to remain at the frontier is heavier, relative to the industry’s age, than anything technology has carried before. Utilities are signing power contracts for gigawatts of capacity that do not exist. 
Meanwhile, Wall Street has started asking a question it ignored a year ago: where, exactly, is the return? In July, efficient Chinese open-weight models showed that frontier-level performance could be reached with a fraction of the compute. AI-linked U.S. equities sold off hard; analysts stepped back from price targets built on the assumption of permanent scarcity. 
China has the mirror-image problem. Chinese companies are trying to close the frontier gap under foreign constraints while having to produce returns large enough to justify the spending at home. In a September study, the Rhodium Group calculated that the combined free cash flow of Chinese tech giants Alibaba, Tencent, and Baidu swung from positive 170 billion yuan in 2025 to negative 16 billion yuan in the first half of 2026. 
The five American hyperscalers saw their own fall from $191 billion to $14 billion and raised $163 billion in long-term debt in six months to keep building. 
Clearly, neither the U.S. nor the Chinese AI sector can fund this race from operations anymore. Both countries’ capital markets are tired of narratives without actual returns. Patience on both sides is wearing thin.
The China-U.S. competition exacerbates these economic dynamics. Each new round of U.S. export controls accelerates the Chinese substitution process, which shrinks the market available for American firms. At the same time, deeper substitution raises the investment China must absorb, which worsens China’s return-on-capital problem. 
In other words, further escalation in the AI race might drain away the capital both systems depends on. This is not a moral argument, but a real financial dilemma. 
Washington and Beijing have already conceded, in their September dialogue, that they face some common risks from AI risks. What’s not clear is whether the economic problem is included on that agenda. 
The November APEC summit offers an unusually practical setting for addressing this issue. The APEC CEO Summit will bring about 1,000 business leaders to Shenzhen with AI on the formal agenda and a Shenzhen Initiative to be released. The host city itself, long nicknamed the Silicon Valley of the East, holds China’s densest cluster of AI and robotics firms. 
Unofficial channels are also in place. Tsinghua’s Center for International Security and Strategy and the Brookings Institution have hosted 14 rounds of China-U.S. AI dialogue since 2019, with Microsoft’s former chief research and strategy officer Craig Mundie serving as a co-chair. 
Three deliverables should be on the agenda for the APEC meeting.
First, China and the United States should add the missing piece of the puzzle in Shenzhen. The official AI dialogue will be held in November; at the APEC summit, both sides can start a standing China-U.S. AI economics dialogue mechanism supported by think tanks and industry associations, the “track two” format long used in China-U.S. exchanges. 
Every official AI conversation so far lacks the people who control the money: finance officials, stock market regulators, and executives. The first such dialogue could take place on the margins of the APEC meeting, convened by think tanks and industry associations rather than ministries. 
In Shenzhen, the Guangdong Artificial Intelligence Industry Association – which operates the Guangdong AI & Robotics Overseas Service Center, the province’s platform for firms going global – could co-convene, alongside established think tanks, a working session between U.S. investors, analysts, and executives and their Guangdong counterparts, on the industry’s own ground. 
Why start with the “track two” format? Because the U.S. and Chinese governments would find it hard to host this conversation. No U.S. administration can openly entertain the thought that its AI boom may be overextended; no Chinese ministry can candidly compare burn rates with a foreign power. Finance officials can talk to economists, and economists can talk to each other. An unofficial venue is the only why this particular talk can happen. 
Second, China and the United States should set a floor under export controls and market access in Shenzhen. Neither side can afford to be seen conducting negotiations over such fundamental issues, but they can quietly exchange red lines in a private setting. Misjudgment, not malice, triggers most crises. The cheapest deterrent is a sentence spoken early. 
Third, it’s time to increase collaborations on the periphery. Standards for AI deployment in third countries – things like data governance, safety evaluation, labor displacement – don’t always pit U.S. and Chinese interests against each other. In fact, that happens far less often than either side assumes. Shenzhen has already hosted APEC-track discussions on responsible AI under the Policy Partnership on Science, Technology and Innovation framework. A joint signal from Washington and Beijing supporting shared regional norms would cost little, match the CEO Summit’s own agenda, and keep third parties from profiting from dueling standards. 
By greenlighting discussions on the economic side of AI, Washington would be shifting a burden, not making a concession. Industry leaders and academic would be the interlocutors, meaning the administration does not need to make more promises even while the Treasury gains more insight into AI’s financial stability.
For its part, Beijing would reinforce its longstanding claim that Chinese AI is an economic project rather than a military one. The talks would also give China’s capital-hungry sector a forum to argue against escalation using commercial – not diplomatic – logic.
The dialogue wouldn’t release a communiqué or joint statement. This would be a recurring conversation that, over time, builds a shared vocabulary for what sustainable AI competition could look like. 
The capital markets are not waiting; they are repricing both countries’ AI sectors now. There’s still a chance for China and the U.S. to get ahead of the bubble, but the window is closing. After the U.S. midterms, coalition politics in Washington will harden, and every unmanaged month afterwards would strengthen the case for constraint in Beijing.
On September 24, the presidents of the United States and China met in Washington and agreed to build what their joint language calls a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” On November 18-19, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet again, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. Two summits in three months is a rare occurrence in China-U.S. relations.
articles.summary: Both sides are feeding an AI investment bubble – and Shenzhen is the place to talk about it.

articles.title: The Mystery of Kyrgyzstan’s Newly Launched Satellite(s)
articles.full_text:
At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. Then the story changed.
Image of Kyrgyzstan’s unnamed, loaf-of-bread-sized nanosatellite.
On October 1, Kyrgyzstan reportedly joined Central Asia’s other spacefaring nations, successfully launching a domestically designed and produced nanosatellite aboard a SpaceX rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California
According to Kyrgyzstan’s government, the unnamed, loaf-of-bread-sized spacecraft weighs 5 kilograms, cost around $130,0000, was equipped with high-resolution cameras, and was — nearly exclusively — the product of domestic innovation. 
The satellite was assembled by two local companies, Kyrgyz Asman and Kyrgyz Electronics, Bishkek stated. The latter company’s director Ilya Cherny did admit that the technology behind the satellite was largely Russian, but pointed out that the team behind its production consisted of 10 homegrown engineers. 
The government also said the satellite would help advance Kyrgyzstan’s top agricultural, environmental, and strategic priorities over its purported 15-year lifespan.
In a statement published on September 24, the country’s Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry stated the satellite’s data would track crop conditions, detect early signs of drought, and monitor glaciers.
Speaking from California on launch day, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said that the country had previously had to pay to obtain this kind of data from other countries, no matter whether it was “information on 100 hectares, 1,000 hectares, or the weather.”
Japarov suggested that the satellite would allow “every square meter” of Kyrgyzstan’s land to be studied to determine its potential arability, while touting the launch as an achievement in national self-sufficiency.
“We did not have our own satellite before… now we will no longer be dependent on [other countries],” Japarov added. “We will control it ourselves 100 percent from Bishkek.”
At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. The country had joined Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and – as of this August – Uzbekistan in the ranks of Central Asia’s spacefarers, largely thanks to its own ingenuity.
The success had been extensively covered in domestic, regional, and international media. And then came a confusing development. 
On October 2, the day after launch, news reports began to include a previously unmentioned detail: the satellite was a joint effort between Kyrgyzstan and the United Arab Emirates.
Three days later, a Kyrgyz news site published a notice that Kyrgyzstan had established a new space monitoring center to receive, process, and utilize data transmitted from the newly launched Altair satellite. 
This was striking for two reasons. First, the name “Altair” had been missing from earlier government press releases. Second – and more importantly – it said the monitoring center would be “provided” data coming from the “UAE-operated” satellite by a body called the Abu Dhabi Maritime Academy. 
Suddenly, Japarov’s claims that Kyrgyzstan would be “no longer dependent” on other countries began to ring hollow.
Not only had Russian technology supposedly been used to design the satellite, but the UAE was apparently going to operate the craft, with Kyrgyzstan merely receiving “access” to its data.
It also didn’t help that Gulf-focused news sites were calling Altair the “first satellite developed and built by UAE engineers,” without even mentioning Bishkek’s involvement in the project.  
What, then, had happened on October 1? Had Kyrgyzstan really launched a satellite of its own making? If so, in what ways were other countries involved? And if the craft launched from California was primarily an Emirati initiative, would Bishkek walk back its claims of national self-sufficiency? 
So far, none of the above questions have been definitively answered. And the matter, described by one prominent regional commentator as a “scandal of cosmic proportions,” has prompted a growing number of increasingly conspiratorial explanations. 
Local news outlet Kaktus Media, for example, suggested that two satellites were likely launched on October 1, one developed by the UAE and one with Russian assistance. (It also noted that Kyrgyzstan’s first satellite initiative, launched in 2019 by a team of all-female engineers, seemed not to be involved, having been wound down previously with no details about the project’s completion.)
Tandyr Media, meanwhile, an independent media outlet known for its popular YouTube channel, drew attention in its video covering the launch to a series of Threads posts by an individual named Dima Balakirev, who claimed to have been personally involved in the satellite project’s development.
In his post, Balakirev appeared to depict himself standing next to a different — much larger — satellite than had been shown in the government’s earlier press releases. Incidentally, the photo also clearly showed a line of text reading “Made in UAE” on one side of the satellite.
According to Balakirev, the spacecraft was a joint project with the UAE, entirely funded “by grants and the Abu Dhabi government,” and was an Earth Remote Sensing satellite – that is, likely the satellite that Japarov was referring to when he was talking about Kyrgyzstan’s newfound capacity to survey itself from above. (Subsequent reporting from government-affiliated sources mentioning the Altair satellite likewise suggested that its data would be used in agricultural planning, water resource management, and environmental monitoring.)
Notably, when questioned by Threads users citing the government’s original (smaller) size specifications, Balakirev insisted that national news outlets had confused two different projects:
“The first is a satellite for Kyrgyzstan, which was assembled in Abu Dhabi. This is a joint project with the UAE, and the Emirates are covering the entire cost. The second is a satellite being built by the team at Kyrgyz Electronics. This is a separate project with its own objectives. The figure of 5 kg and 10–12 million soms [$114,350 – $137,200] refers specifically to this one.” 
Although Balakirev’s exact title and position are unknown, as Tandyr Media pointed out, the self-described “entrepreneur and techie” appeared to have been present in California alongside Japarov, and shared Instagram stories from the event. 
Given all that, as Tandyr host Dmitriy Lozhnikov himself concluded, what is left now is a substantially muddied picture. 
According to one possible version of events, Kyrgyzstan did launch its smaller, unnamed bread-loaf-sized satellite, whose function is not entirely clear, on October 1. On the same day, meanwhile, the larger, UAE-designed Altair satellite also launched from California – data from which Bishkek has confirmed it is now paying to access.
In another plausible version, proposed by emigre political scientist Aidarbek Raev, the Kyrgyz-designed nanosatellite might not have been launched at all, which would mean that reports of Kyrgyzstan’s national technological achievements have been greatly exaggerated.
articles.summary: At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. Then the story changed.

articles.title: South Korea Recalls Ambassador, Demands Public Apology From Ukraine
articles.full_text:
A diplomatic rift is growing after a North Korean prisoner transfer that Kyiv revealed against Seoul’s wishes.
South Korea decided on October 8 to recall Ambassador Park Ki-chang from Ukraine. It’s Seoul’s first ambassador recall since 2008, when South Korea withdrew its envoy from Japan over a territorial claim to the Dokdo islets. 
The decision came 15 days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly. Seoul says the two governments had agreed to keep the transfer confidential. However, Kyiv first denied any such agreement before its Foreign Ministry attributed the dispute to differing interpretations.
The two soldiers at the center of the dispute were captured in January 2025 in the Kursk region of Russia. North Korea had sent troops there to support the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The captured soldiers arrived in South Korea in mid-September after saying they wished to settle there.
Zelenskyy’s public announcement of their arrival drew a response from South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on September 24 in a post on the social platform X. He called the disclosure deeply regrettable. Lee also cited the problems that disclosure could cause.
Kyiv rejected that account the next day. Dmytro Lytvyn, a communications adviser to Zelenskyy, denied that any confidentiality agreement existed.
The South Korean presidential office voiced strong regret over the disclosure and Ukraine’s denial on September 27. It demanded an official explanation and apology. It also signaled that additional measures were under consideration. Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said that Ukraine’s had sought the secrecy itself. He added that Kyiv had cited possible criticism at home for giving up a chance to swap the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners held by Russia.
The next day, First Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo summoned Andrii Vieshkin, who is Ukraine’s acting ambassador in Seoul. The vice minister repeated the demands to him.
Still, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the dispute on October 1 as a diplomatic misunderstanding. Sybiha did not offer the public apology that Seoul had demanded.
In a post on X the next day, Lee wrote that Ukraine had made the South Korean head of state a “liar” by denying the agreement. He also warned of further measures unless Kyiv publicly apologized.
Lee also broadened his criticism to remarks by Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian presidential office. Budanov had warned in an interview on September 27 that tension along the inter-Korean border was rising by the day. Days earlier, suspected North Korean mines had exploded inside the Demilitarized Zone between the two Koreas and wounded three South Korean soldiers. So Lee accused Kyiv of speaking of an imminent clash between the two Koreas as if wishing for war. 
On October 6, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told lawmakers that a message from Ukraine had included words of apology. However, he said it fell somewhat short of the expectations of Seoul.
Kyiv characterized the message differently. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said on October 7 that Ukraine had expressed regret over the public criticism between the two countries. The spokesperson also attributed the dispute to differing interpretations of the confidentiality arrangement.
A separate dispute surfaced in the same week. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the presidential commissioner of Ukraine for sanctions policy, said on October 6 that fuel shipments from South Korean ports had helped Russia offset refinery losses caused by Ukrainian strikes. The South Korean presidential office rejected the claim on October 7.
In the announcement recalling Ambassador Park the next day, the South’s Foreign Ministry said it hoped to settle pending issues through continued consultations with Ukraine.
The Foreign Ministry of Ukraine responded that diplomacy should prevail over emotions. Tykhyi added that diplomatic efforts were underway through private channels. 
Seoul had good reasons to want the transfer kept quiet. According to Seoul, the families of the two men remain in North Korea, where they could face reprisals over their relatives’ decision to defect. 
The National Intelligence Service also told lawmakers on September 30 that the disclosure appeared aimed at building public support in South Korea for arms supplies to Ukraine. Seoul has supported Ukraine with financial and humanitarian aid but not with lethal weapons, even after North Korea began sending tens of thousands of soldiers to fight for Russia.
If Ukraine’s government was hoping to bolster its image with South Koreans, it badly miscalculated. Instead, Kyiv has lost the trust of Seoul, and the harm cannot be repaired in private. Because the disclosure was public, a message passed between ministers cannot solve the problem. 
Meanwhile another Ukrainian official opened a second dispute. Vlasiuk raised the fuel claim on October 6 while Seoul was still waiting for an apology. The South Korean government says petroleum products are not on its list of controlled exports. Whatever the merits, the claim muddied a dispute that Kyiv had started. The fuel question belongs in a separate channel on sanctions compliance.
With that question set aside, Seoul has demanded three things. Kyiv should acknowledge that a confidentiality agreement existed. The Ukrainian government should offer an official, public apology. And Kyiv should commit to steps that prevent a recurrence. 
Park may return to Kyiv only after Ukraine does all three.

articles.title: Australia’s Billionaire Problem and the ‘Corruption of the Democratic Process’
articles.full_text:
Australia’s incoming political finance laws will cap donations and electioneering spending for the first time, but the limits are generous, the rules complex, and the two-year delay suspiciously convenient for the major parties.
A truck part of a political fundraising campaign organized by the far-right populist One Nation party, criticizing the incumbent Labor Albanese government.
Mining magnate Gina Rinehart and close associates have reportedly gifted over AU$3 million to the One Nation Party in the last financial year, in cash and even an entire aircraft. “Reportedly,” as none of this has to be declared publicly until February 2027.
Clive Palmer splurged over AU$260 million on electioneering at the last three national polls, and then some. The land of the “fair go” has never been as egalitarian as it thinks. As long as billionaires dress down and speak rough, they can speak with a loud hailer and burn money to inflate their interests.
Yet even before the billionaires, Australia had a money-in-electoral-politics problem.
The two parties of government, Labor and Liberal, have been running business “forums” or “networks” and charging over AU$100,000 for membership, permitting access to front-benchers at regular gatherings. The electoral commission even held, bafflingly, that these sums were not disclosable “gifts,” because they bought something of value. That is the very form of privileged access that most citizens believe corrupts the democratic process.
Current national laws are laissez-faire, by world standards. Disclosure, as noted, is rooted in an untimely model from the paper-and-pen era of the 1980s. And it only applies to “gifts” over AU$17,300 per annum. Unlike the majority of states, there have been no caps on donations – aside from recent bans on “foreign source” donations, inspired by fears of Chinese influence. Nor have there been caps on national electioneering spending.
Hence the Rinehart, Palmer, and party network examples have all been lawful. And parties at the national level have long enjoyed public funding – “clean money,” but it has been extra cream rather than compensation for any limits.
That legal permissiveness is set to change, from sometime next year. For the first time, party and lobby group electioneering at national elections will be capped. So too will donations. Disclosure of donations will be at a lower level, and closer to “real time.” The change has been a long time coming.
The new laws – around 250 pages, including transitional rules – were the result of protracted negotiations across 2024. They passed in early 2025 with support from the Coalition. One upside of this is that buy-in, from both major parties, means the principles underlying caps and transparency are accepted for the foreseeable future.
This doesn’t mean the laws are ideal. The Greens support the principles, but (rightly) decry that the caps are too generous. The headline cap prevents donations of more than AU$50,000 to one political entity. But that obscures the ability to donate that amount to each division of a nationally organized party, several of its candidates and even a couple of sympathetic lobby groups. The effective cap is more like AU$1.6 million per annum.
The spending cap will be AU$90 million for a national party. That’s roughly at the Palmer level, which in his hands was both a record and a turnoff for voters. Within that total cap, there is a limit of AU$800,000 per targeted, marginal seat campaign. The “Teal” independents say that all the caps need redrafting, alleging unfairness to them. Party candidates benefit from the nationwide spending of their party, promoting its brand, policies, and leadership. Also, parties can fund that wider campaign with multiple donations from a single source, something independents cannot. There is a legitimate concern that rules shouldn’t artificially shield established parties, at a time when party politics is realigning.
Lobby groups will face an AU$11.25 million “electioneering” cap. So sugar daddies of the Teals will be able to do background electioneering supporting them. Interest groups will also still be able to mount unlimited single interest campaigns, providing they just promote their policy interests rather than boosting or attacking parties or candidates.
All-in-all, the new laws are better than nothing, if far from ideal. First, the limits are exceedingly generous. No one wants parties to be starved of resources. Party democracy beats billionaires directly campaigning – like Bloomberg and Musk in the U.S. party machines, however derided, have an ongoing interest in their long-term reputation. Channeling donations through parties, in the Australian way, insulates against corruption. It is far easier to buy a self-interested individual politician, as U.S. experience also shows.
The new laws will dampen the ability of incumbent and business friendly parties to rely on mega-donations, from corporations or unions, into their campaign budgets. In return, the regime will ramp up public funding to AU$5 per vote – or AU$10 per elector given we have House and Senate votes. In addition, mimicking state practice, parties (and independent MPs) will get a second flow of subsidies. In the form of “administrative” assistance, paid at a metric based on the number of Commonwealth MPs they have.
Second, the new laws are unduly complex. Admittedly, regulating the flow of money is hard. There are waterbed effects. So, to mix metaphors, regulation engages in a cat-and-mouse game. But these laws numb my brain, and I’ve spent 30 years studying the area. Parties, especially small or new ones, rely on volunteers at ground level. Not all can afford legal advice. The electoral commission will do well to focus not on missteps by small fry, but on lurks by the well-to-do and well-advised.
Finally, why is there a two-year delay for the new restraints and obligations to come into effect? The official explanation is that the commission needs time to gear up the new disclosure portal and educate itself and others as to the new complexities. One doesn’t have to be too cynical, though, to suspect another motive. Seeing Rinehart shower big money on One Nation – and its explosion in the polls – the major parties want time to catch up, to fill their election coffers ahead of a late 2027 or early 2028 poll.  As St. Augustine quipped, “Lord make me chaste; just not yet.”
One thing to watch for is unintended effects. Will big money just reappear in other guises? Palmer, capped in what he can give to his own party, may just run more oblique campaigns directly through a corporate vehicle. Unions and business groups too may campaign more nakedly to help Labor and the Coalition. Astro-turfed groups may appear to strain the law.
Ultimately, there is no perfect regime of regulating money in electoral politics. Integrity values, the ideals of political equality and liberty, and the pragmatic need for fair party resourcing, have to be accommodated. Being part of a cat-and-mouse game, the new laws will inevitably be revisited by the end of the decade.
Originally published under Creative Commons by 360info™.

articles.title: The China-EU Trade Truce Buys Time
articles.full_text:
For the EU, the choice is increasingly difficult: secure real concessions from Beijing to address structural trade imbalances or deploy stronger unilateral measures to protect its industrial base.
EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shake hands after their talks in Beijing, China, Oct, 9, 2026.
Like last month’s summit between the U.S. and Chinese presidents, the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultations in Beijing were primarily about stabilization rather than a breakthrough. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao closed a handful of agreements and confirmed that neither side wants a trade war. However, the structural issues remain unresolved. What both sides gained is time. 
For the European Union, the choice is increasingly difficult: secure real concessions from Beijing to address structural trade imbalances or deploy stronger unilateral measures to protect its industrial base. Compounding this dilemma is Europe’s risk of becoming an adjustment variable in the China-U.S. strategic competition, absorbing diverted Chinese exports when tensions escalate while losing market opportunities and negotiating leverage when Washington and Beijing strike bilateral deals. Washington holds the technology lever, while Beijing controls critical minerals and key nodes of global supply chains. Europe depends on both.
The most concrete outcome of the talks concerns the automotive sector. Under a preliminary deal, Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU could be curbed more than half against projected levels over the next four years. The stakes are high. In 2025, the EU imported more than 1 million Chinese-made cars, worth $15.5 billion (13.7 billion euros) and up 30 percent in volume on 2024. Hybrids tell the story best: 659 Chinese hybrids sold in the EU in 2022, versus more than 160,000 in the first seven months of 2026, plus almost 218,000 plug-in hybrids.
Chinese brands now hold almost 12 percent of Europe’s new-car market, up from 1 percent five years ago, and roughly a third of plug-in hybrid sales. In the United States, Chinese cars are absent. Washington has effectively shut Chinese electric vehicles out of its market through 100 percent tariffs, while Europe remains far more exposed to Chinese automotive imports. The U.S., a market of 16.2 million new vehicles, bought fewer than 90,000 China-made vehicles in 2024, almost all of them Western brands built in China.
The rapid expansion of Chinese carmakers has intensified competitive pressures on European manufacturers, particularly in Germany and France, which had pushed for tougher trade measures. The proposed 50 percent reduction in Chinese hybrid exports is a step forward, but it is measured against projected growth, not current volumes.
China’s hybrid expansion accelerated after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese battery-electric vehicles in 2024. Manufacturers shifted toward hybrids, which were exempt from those duties. While Washington imposed steep barriers to Chinese electric vehicles, Brussels left a significant loophole. The hybrid cars deal is therefore less a breakthrough than an attempt to correct a weakness in Europe’s trade policy.
As for whether the deal will work, much will depend on enforcement. Effective restrictions could give European automakers time to adjust. Weak implementation would allow Chinese exports to expand further, forcing Brussels to consider tougher measures and risking retaliation that could disrupt supply chains and investment on both sides. Meanwhile, Chinese automakers are increasingly moving from exports to manufacturing inside Europe. The strategic question is no longer simply how many Chinese cars are imported in the European market, but where industrial value is created, who controls the technology, and where the jobs are located. 
The second result concerns market access and trade rebalancing. Brussels and Beijing agreed to cut tariffs on a range of EU products to the most-favored-nation (MFN) rates set under WTO rules. The goods covered, from car parts to olive oil and footwear, account for nearly $4.7 billion in exports. If implemented, the measure would save European exporters at least $260 million in duties.
Set against the trade figures, however, it is a small gain. In her State of the Union speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the EU’s deficit with China “unsustainable.” It now runs at more than 1 billion euros a day. The goods deficit rose from 306 billion euros in 2024 to 360 billion euros in 2025 and could reach 400 billion euros ($470 billion) this year, according to Eurostat.
The United States, meanwhile, moved in the opposite direction. In 2025, its goods deficit with China fell by almost a third to $202 billion, the lowest in two decades, as imports from China dropped 30 percent. China’s share of U.S. imports fell to about 9 percent, the lowest since it joined the WTO in 2001. The EU’s goods deficit with China is now twice America’s. What Washington kept out with tariffs, Europe increasingly absorbs. 
Sefcovic defended the new deal with China as the result of an intense negotiation, noting that Washington had needed far more rounds to get its own deal. But he warned against complacency.
The third result concerns critical raw materials, above all rare earths and permanent magnets. This is where Europe depends on China most – 98 percent of EU demand for rare earth magnets is met by Chinese imports. Beijing will ease export licensing for European companies through a green channel. That matters for carmakers, renewables, and defense. But Beijing keeps control of the licenses, and with it the power to turn supplies on and off. 
Washington got more. At the Busan summit in October 2025, the United States secured a one-year suspension of China’s new export restrictions and general licenses for its companies. The White House summit in September 2026 extended that suspension until January 10, 2027. Brussels obtained faster procedures for licenses that remain individual and revocable. Washington negotiated with tariffs and semiconductor controls on the table. Europe only trade-defense tools it has yet to use. 
The industrial strategies differ as well. The United States has stepped up directly, with the Pentagon taking a stake in MP Materials and Washington forging minerals deals with Australia and Japan. Europe is relying on the Critical Raw Materials Act and RESourceEU, a sound framework but slower and less funded. Faster licenses make Europe’s supplies more predictable, but they do not make it less dependent.
That’s not to say Europe has no leverage. Four days before the talks, France and Germany jointly called for stronger trade defense instruments against Chinese overcapacity, subsidies, and market distortions. Beijing got the message. In response, official Beijing urged Paris and Berlin not to push the EU toward protectionist tools. Germany’s position carried the most weight. The European Commission went to Beijing with more leverage than before.

The rare earth agreement eases Chinese exports that the same carmakers rely on. Europe wants fewer of some Chinese goods and a steady supply of others, and on both counts the decision rests with Beijing. The recent truce calms the relationship but leaves the imbalances in place.

articles.title: Southeast Asia Has a Serious Drug Problem
articles.full_text:
Southeast Asia’s drug labs are pumping out unprecedented amounts of meth and other synthetic drugs.
In June 2025, anti-drug police in Thailand descended on a small tourist boat moored at a pier in Rayong, a seaside town south of Bangkok. Aboard the ship, inside plastic bags disguised as corn flour packages, they found an alarming cargo: 2.4 metric tons of crystal methamphetamine. This one shipment, bound for overseas markets, was bigger than the entire annual total of meth seizures that Thailand made in 2016. An official from the Department of Special Investigation later told the press that the shipment was worth an estimated $9.15 million – and would sell for ten times that once it hit foreign shores.
Thailand’s meth bust was just the tip of the iceberg. Just a few weeks before that, authorities in Indonesia seized a cargo ship near Batam Island, just south of Singapore. On board they found a similar haul: 2.1 tons of crystal meth. It was the largest drug confiscation in Indonesia’s history.
There were more mega-seizures in late 2025 and early 2026. In September 2025, authorities in Yangon confiscated 1.8 metric tons of crystal meth and 4 million methamphetamine tablets, which authorities said were set to be smuggled to Malaysia. In February 2026, Malaysia confiscated 76 sacks of crystal meth, totaling around 1.5 tons, from two vessels off the east coast of peninsular Malaysia. Two months after that, Thai authorities confiscated 2 metric tons hidden in a pickup truck en route to a port in eastern Thailand.
According to experts, all of these meth shipments originated in the Golden Triangle, the rugged region where Thailand’s borders converge with those of Myanmar and Laos. For decades the Golden Triangle has been associated with narcotics – initially heroin, synthesized from the poppies that grow well in the region’s cool upland climate.
But over the past decade, the Southeast Asian drug trade has shifted decisively toward synthetic drugs – particularly methamphetamine. These are cheaper to make, easier to transport, and not dependent on the weather for a good harvest.
Southeast Asia’s drug labs are now pumping out unprecedented amounts of meth. According to the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime – or UNODC – regional seizures of methamphetamine hit a new record of 349 tons in 2025, up from 236 tons the year before. In 2015, regional seizures captured just 65 tons. And these drugs are being sold all around the world.
The UNODC says that last year, Southeast Asia accounted for around 94 percent of all the methamphetamine seizures  in the entire world. The UN agency reported an “immense volume of methamphetamine trafficked through land-based and maritime routes.”
Everybody knows that drug seizures represent only a small fraction of the total amount of drugs being trafficked through the region. Southeast Asia is facing down the biggest drug crisis in its history.

articles.title: Trump’s Targeting of Indian IT Firms Hits India-US Ties Again
articles.full_text:
Washington announced last week that it would not accept or process applications from top Indian IT companies for H-1B visas.
Infosys headquarters in Bangalore, India.
Ties between India and the United States hit another bump last week with the Trump administration freezing green card requests from eight technology firms, including those from India.
U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced on October 8 that Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Capgemini, Microsoft, and Adobe have been suspended from participating in the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM), a program that is largely used by technology companies and outsourcing firms to sponsor a foreign worker’s permanent residency in the U.S. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.
The announcement came weeks before U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to New Delhi.
Indian IT companies appear largely unperturbed by the U.S. policy change. Infosys, India’s second-largest IT firm, said it did ‌not anticipate a material impact from the PERM application suspension. The National Association of Software and Service Companies (NASSCOM), India’s IT industry body, said that Indian companies had significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas in recent years and had expanded their local ‌hiring ⁠in the U.S. Relatively few workers move from H-1B visas to permanent residency through PERM, it said.
Ajay Srivastava, who heads the Global Trade Research Initiative, a New Delhi-based trade and commerce think tank, said the U.S. move was a “warning for India’s IT industry.” “It covers four leading Indian IT firms and disrupts the permanent-residency plans of their employees, making long-term staffing in the U.S. more uncertain,” Srivastava told The Diplomat.
“The larger concern is India’s dependence on a market that accounts for 54.1 percent of its software and IT-enabled services exports. The measure signals a more protectionist U.S. approach to foreign technology workers. India should prepare for possible restrictions extending beyond green card sponsorship,” he said, adding that Indian firms should widen their export markets to reduce their vulnerability to sudden U.S. policy changes.
India’s software services exports to the U.S. fetched $221.4 billion in revenues in 2025-26, an 8.2 percent year-on-year increase.
Adding salt to injury was a comment by Vice President J.D. Vance. Speaking to reporters after Sonderling’s announcement, Vance said: “Our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
In a sharply worded statement, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said that “talent mobility adds value to both economies.” The measures announced by the United States “do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries.” Recalling that the U.S. was a country built by immigrants, the statement said that “resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive.” The allusion was to India’s British colonial rulers transporting more than a million Indians to work as contract labor in British colonies abroad after the abolition of slavery by the British in 1833.
There is speculation in India that the U.S. policy change on green card requests is aimed at showing President Donald Trump’s domestic audience that his administration is tough on immigration. The U.S. will vote in mid-term elections in November. Voters are reportedly unhappy with the Trump administration’s performance, especially on the handling of the economy, with job numbers falling short of expectations.
Last week’s restrictions on Indian IT companies, together with Vance’s comments, have added to the chill in India-U.S. relations, especially since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
A trade pact negotiated between the two sides remains unsigned despite many rounds of talks. Washington’s courting of Pakistan, which India sees as instigating terrorism against it, has not gone down well in Delhi.
Speaking at the Asia Society in New York in September, India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar highlighted the U.S. anti-immigration push affecting the movement of Indian workers to the U.S. as among the main causes for the current strain in bilateral ties.
Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has implemented several measures to rework American immigration policy. These include bestowing more powers on officials to enforce domestic immigration laws as well as increasing anti-immigration raids and deportations. Last year, India accepted the return of almost 400 of its nationals deported by the Trump administration. Their arrival in India in military aircraft and in shackles caused a domestic outcry.
The Trump administration has also been squeezing the H-1B visa program that allows foreign nationals to temporarily work in the U.S. in specialty occupations for a maximum of six years. In August, Washington proposed a regulation to raise the fee on new H-1B visas to over $100,000. The ​H-1B program offers 65,000 visas annually, allowing American employers to hire highly skilled workers with specialty training. The program permits another 20,000 visas for workers with advanced degrees for a three-to-six-year period. Fees for the two categories of visas were between $2,000 and $5,000 earlier.
Trump’s proposed regulation was struck down by a California court in September, blocking the $100,000 fee tag. India has been the largest beneficiary of the H-1B visas program for many years.
With the U.S. narrowing the options for skilled Indian workers, the Indian government could look at asking American companies to follow the examples of Microsoft and Adobe and set up Global Capability Centers in India. These centers are offshore units set up by companies to deliver services for their parent organizations.
India presently has more than 2,100 centers employing 2.36 ​million people and generating nearly $100 billion in revenue. The Indian government is also looking to attract Indian workers currently employed in the U.S. to return home.
The denial of green cards under PERM is likely to figure in talks when Rubio, the U.S. secretary of state and national security adviser, arrives in India later this month. Also likely to figure in the agenda is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” which authorizes Trump to sanction countries that buy oil from Russia and Iran. India is among the largest purchasers of Russian oil. Given that the U.S. itself is looking to import diesel from Russia, India is likely to seek clarification on the provisions of the Lindsay Graham Act should it import fuel from Russia.
People-to-people relations have always been the strongest anchor of India-U.S. bilateral ties. Washington’s latest move hits this anchor. Rubio and Jaishankar have a challenging agenda before them.

articles.title: Why Did the Industrial Revolution Not Start in India?
articles.full_text:
Due to abundant labor, its social structure, and the inertia of an economic system, there was little incentive to initiate mechanization and the Industrial Revolution in India.
An illustration depicting the Industrial Revolution in Birmingham, England.
Historians often ask why the Industrial Revolution began in Europe and not elsewhere.
The classical framing of this question is the Needham Problem. Writing in 1969, the British historian of science, Joseph Needham, asked: “Why did modern science, the mathematization of hypotheses about Nature, with all its implications for advanced technology, take its meteoric rise only in the West…[and] had not developed in Chinese civilization?” After all, Needham noted, “between the first century BC and the fifteenth century AD, Chinese civilization was much more efficient than occidental in applying human natural knowledge to practical human needs.”
The Industrial Revolution refers to the transformation from agrarian, handicraft economies to machine- and factory-based industrial economies. It began in the 18th century and was the harbinger of the modern world, enabling Western dominance over most of the rest of the world, either through outright colonization, as in much of India and Africa, or by means of indirect control, as in China and Iran. The Industrial Revolution built on the preceding Scientific Revolution in Europe, which emphasized the acquisition of knowledge through reason and empirical research.
Needham sought to answer the question of why the Industrial Revolution did not begin outside Europe by examining the evolution of science in China.
But the issue ought not to be seen as merely a dichotomy between Western and Chinese civilization. In fact, India and the Islamic world would arguably have been better candidates than China for the emergence of industrial civilization. As in Europe, large swathes of India and the Islamic world engaged in long-distance trade, patronized universities, and were divided into competing kingdoms fighting against each other and against pastoralist peoples from the neighboring steppes and deserts. The Islamic world and Europe, especially, had to compensate for a lack of abundant labor. Incessant warfare led to the adaptation of gunpowder, while trade spread innovations such as the compass and paper beyond the region.
In India, there are two periods that stand out as optimal times for an industrial revolution to occur there. The first is in the 6ht century CE, when the Gupta Empire had disintegrated into a plethora of kingdoms and a shared elite culture across polities emerged. India thus experienced both political competition and was home to a pan-India culture. An exchange of ideas happened at a number of universities, such as Nalanda. These conditions were similar to those in early modern Europe. Some of India’s greatest advances in the arts, philosophy, and mathematics occurred in the centuries following the end of the Gupta Empire, with figures like mathematician Brahmagupta and philosopher Shankara living during this period.
A second period would have been in the Deccan peninsula during the early modern era. The topography and location of this region favored the persistence of several rival kingdoms seeking to gain an advantage over each other. They all had access to ocean-going trade and had a history of trade guilds, which allowed the easy flow of goods and ideas. In the early 16th century, the Deccan sultanates were some of the earliest innovators in cannon technology and military architecture. In the 18th century, the Kingdom of Mysore invented sophisticated rockets and other weaponry, whilst the Marathas established ordnance factories where skilled metalworkers created cannon and firearms adapted to local Indian conditions.
While it should be noted that the engine behind 18th-century Deccani manufacturing were skilled craftsmen rather than mechanization, the region had many of the right ingredients to commence industrialization around the same time as in Europe. The British conquest halted these initial local moves in that direction.
However, there were many other reasons the Industrial Revolution began in northwest Europe — and not elsewhere, such as in India — in the 18th century.
Industrialization is not inevitable. It is not the default outcome of human civilization. It takes certain institutions and worldviews as prerequisites and particular economic and geopolitical conditions — many of which came together by chance — to spark the process.
A great many factors must align, not least intense international rivalry in the state’s vicinity. For example, a polity ought to have enough labor to man its factories, but not too much labor — as China did — so as to make investment in industry more expensive than utilizing manual labor. A polity would ideally be sedentary rather than nomadic, stable enough internally to guarantee the continuity of institutions such as universities, companies, and land ownership, and home to a flexible labor market: the masses of peasants in many states were not permitted to move freely and offer their services anywhere. The polity must be strong enough to guarantee the rule of law, but not so bureaucratic so as to stifle private enterprise and innovation.
The historian Kyle Harper, speaking about the Roman Empire, noted that: “there [were] tinkerers and engineers, but they [were not] talking to the mathematicians and the physicists. If you were from on high to design self-sustaining innovation, I think you would want to bring those elements into proximity.” Harper argues that industrialization took off in early modern Europe because states funded scientific research and married the findings to the work of engineers and builders. Both groups seeded each other’s minds with ideas.
This process requires a state — or well-endowed institutions, such as corporations and universities — to facilitate scientific discoveries and its practical applications. This is a time- and capital-intensive process that was undertaken — more often than not — to improve the finances and security of the state through gains in efficiency and production. The benefits had to have been more than the costs.
On top of that, the state must overcome tradition and inertia: not an easy task. For example, after the victory of the Vijayanagara Empire against the Sultanate of Bijapur in 1520 at the Battle of Raichur, the two sides drew different conclusions on the efficiency of gunpowder.
Writing about the emperor of Vijayanagara, Krishadevaraya, historian Richard Eaton notes:
Though impressed with the matchlocks used by his Portuguese mercenaries, [Krishnadevaraya] failed to see firearms as the way of the future…there is no evidence that he followed up his victories by establishing an arsenal or a matchlock foundry in Vijayanagara. Nor did he or his successors ever mount cannon on the walls of their capital or provincial forts, or in other ways adapt their defensive systems to accommodate gunpowder technology…Bijapur, by contrast, responded quite differently to the battle’s outcome…[and] therefore launched an accelerated drive to pioneer new gunpowder technologies…from the small swivel guns that the Portuguese had placed on the gunwales of their ships, they took the idea of mounting a much larger cannon on a cubic block of granite set on an iron pin, enabling the gun to move horizontally.
Inertia is difficult to overcome. Research has found that in many parts of India, even when women are offered high-paying jobs in factories or offices, they decline due to family pressure and tradition that looks down on women working outside of the home. And for cultural reasons related to status, many Indians dream of becoming government bureaucrats or white-collar workers in the information technology industry, rather than seeking to work in factories or engaging in commerce or sales. These factors inhabit industrialization, development, and the spread of rational socioeconomic organization deriving from individualism.
For these reasons, for much of human history, it has been more efficient for most states — and most elites — to simply exploit land and people harder and harder. The Romans had a copious number of slaves and empires as diverse as the Ottomans and Mughals engaged in tax farming: the practice of a government contracting tax collection to private individuals, individuals who would often take a cut for themselves after fleecing peasants and merchants.
Many scholars have speculated that in India, mathematicians, artisans, scientists and builders were not often in the business of exchanging ideas, belonging to different endogamous jatis, or castes. According to economic historian Tirthankar Roy, “technology existed as tacit knowledge of artisan communities, and the evidence of partnership between diverse skills was rare. Scientific knowledge was often documented, but remained restricted within scholastic circles.”
Contrary to a widespread but incorrect belief, literacy was widespread amongst a number of castes, and was not restricted to just Brahmins. But different communities still interacted with and circulated texts mostly within their social milieu, and sometimes different jatis even used different writing systems. For example, in parts of North India, merchants used the Mahajani alphabet, scribes (Kayasthas) used the Kaithi alphabet, and Brahmins used Devanagari.
Another factor that may have inhibited industrialization in pre-modern India was its abundant quantity of specialized and cheap labor, which dampens the need for mechanization and labor-saving devices. China, too, had abundant labor, and thus, less incentive to mechanize in pre-modern times. The first Mughal Emperor Babur famously observed this phenomenon in his diary, the Baburnameh:
Another good thing in Hindustan is that it has unnumbered and endless workmen of every kind. There is a fixed caste (jam’i) for every sort of work and for every thing, which has done that work or that thing from father to son till now…680 men worked daily on my buildings in Agra and of Agra stone-cutters only; while 1491 stone-cutters worked daily on my buildings in Agra, Sikri, Biana, Dulpur, Gwalior, and Kuil. In the same way there are numberless artisans and workmen of every sort in Hindustan.
In fact, it was arguably not in the interests of a state to create a large number of unemployed people by introducing industry. Even today, if one were to observe construction in much of India, one would see a large number of individuals carrying and laying bricks with their bare hands instead of using machines or complex tools.
The historian Ada Palmer has noted that industrialization was less likely to begin in richer regions with more developed artisanal industries and vibrant trade, such as Italy. In fact, as per Palmer, even though Italians during the Renaissance had the technology for industrial looms, they did not want to pivot away from producing artisanal fabrics, which brought them wealth.
The parallels with India are striking. Due to its abundant labor, its social structure, and the inertia of an economic system that worked well enough, there was little incentive to initiate mechanization and the Industrial Revolution in India. The parts of India that came closest to industrialization — such as states in the early modern Deccan — did so when geopolitical conditions highly incentivized such an outcome. Survival trumped inaction in those cases. But more often than not, it was too late, or unnecessary, as the Industrial Revolution arrived fully formed from Europe in India.
Historians often ask why the Industrial Revolution began in Europe and not elsewhere.
The classical framing of this question is the Needham Problem. Writing in 1969, the British historian of science, Joseph Needham, asked: “Why did modern science, the mathematization of hypotheses about Nature, with all its implications for advanced technology, take its meteoric rise only in the West…[and] had not developed in Chinese civilization?” After all, Needham noted, “between the first century BC and the fifteenth century AD, Chinese civilization was much more efficient than occidental in applying human natural knowledge to practical human needs.”
The Industrial Revolution refers to the transformation from agrarian, handicraft economies to machine- and factory-based industrial economies. It began in the 18th century and was the harbinger of the modern world, enabling Western dominance over most of the rest of the world, either through outright colonization, as in much of India and Africa, or by means of indirect control, as in China and Iran. The Industrial Revolution built on the preceding Scientific Revolution in Europe, which emphasized the acquisition of knowledge through reason and empirical research.
articles.summary: Due to abundant labor, its social structure, and the inertia of an economic system, there was little incentive to initiate mechanization and the Industrial Revolution in India.

articles.title: To Rebuild the Nepali Congress, Gagan Thapa Must First Reform It
articles.full_text:
Recently re-elected president of the Nepali Congress, Thapa vowed to end the culture of nepotism and groupism in the party and to open it to a new generation of leaders.
Gagan Thapa addresses the Nepali Congress party’s 15th general convention in Kathmandu, Nepal, Oct. 5, 2026.
Among the most charismatic political leaders of his generation, Gagan Thapa was long talked of as a prime minister-in-waiting. As he rose up the ranks of the Nepali Congress — the social democratic party that has been the country’s dominant political force for most of the post-1990 period — this advocate of value-based politics with unmatched oratory skills seemed destined to lead his party and country.
Then came the Gen Z movement. In just two days of protests in September 2025, the movement upended the old political order. K.P. Oli, the communist prime minister at the time, had to run for his life. The top Congress leader, Sher Bahadur Deuba, was beaten black and blue. Along with the homes of hundreds of other political leaders, Thapa’s Kathmandu home was torched and he too had to go into hiding.
The Gen Z movement would also act as a catalyst for change in the Congress. In its aftermath, a set of second-generation leaders under Thapa finally dared to revolt and wrest party leadership away from Deuba, then age 79. Yet most Nepalis saw this as too little, too late, and the Congress under Thapa performed dismally in the first post-uprising national polls held in March 2026.
Today, the Congress is a diminished force, occupying just 38 seats in the 275-member lower House. Meanwhile, with 182 seats, the new Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), which took ownership of the Gen Z movement, garnered a near two-thirds majority.
When the Congress was trounced in the March 2026 polls, old party leaders put the blame for the defeat on Thapa and his “mistimed” revolt that was orchestrated on the eve of the March elections. But the RSP was riding a wave of discontent with the established political parties, and Congress under its old leadership would arguably have fared even worse in the elections.
Now Thapa, 50, has been re-elected party president by its just-concluded general convention. While asking for votes, he vowed to end the culture of nepotism and groupism in the party and to open the outfit to a new generation of leaders.
His other proposals include a system of primaries to pick the party’s electoral candidates and amending the constitution charter to limit any individual to two terms as prime minister. Thapa’s proposed reforms, if implemented, could open up new democratic space, both in the party and in the national polity.
This is in sharp contrast to the centralizing and power-hoarding tendencies of Sher Bahadur Deuba, the erstwhile party president, who did much to discredit the image of a party that was long associated with principled leaders like B.P. Koirala and Ganesh Man Singh.
But Thapa has a monumental challenge on his hands. The RSP has captured much of the political space once occupied by the Congress. Under party chair Rabi Lamichhane and senior leader Balendra Shah, who is also Nepal’s prime minister, the RSP remains very popular. It is thus expected to replicate its federal poll success in the local and provincial elections scheduled for 2027.
The old rivalry between Congress, the old champion of liberal democratic values, and the communists appears increasingly irrelevant to Nepali voters today. Now it is upon Thapa’s party to show the skeptical electorate what liberal democratic values mean in practice, and why a reformed Congress can uphold them.
The other big challenge for Thapa would be to bring back into the party’s fold the disgruntled leaders who still back former party president Deuba. If a big chunk of old Congress stalwarts continue to side with Deuba, Thapa will have a tough time rebuilding the party organization. His efforts to reinvigorate the Congress will be dealt a further blow if the Supreme Court, which is currently considering a case on the legality of the Thapa-led Congress, chooses to identify the Deuba faction as the authentic Congress party.
Gagan Thapa has many strengths. He has worked his way up the ranks of the Congress. However, Thapa’s rise came even as the party’s top leaders were openly engaging in self-centered politics and corruption. In the eyes of many young Nepalis, he preferred to play it safe and bided his time. But Nepali youths were less patient — and revolted. Many thus reckon Thapa’s time has passed.
Whether or not that is true, it is important for the Congress under Thapa to continue to be electorally competitive in Nepali politics. Besides its role as the champion of liberal democratic values, a strong Congress will also make the RSP accountable.
With the discrediting of the Congress under the old leadership, the RSP has come to occupy the liberal democratic space without doing much to demonstrate its commitment to liberal values. In just six months in office, the new RSP government has taken a number of questionable decisions — from removing squatters without due process to jailing political leaders on flimsy legal grounds — that make people suspect the party’s democratic credentials.
Thapa has proven his credentials as a fighter for democratic rights, as a competent administrator during his tenure as health minister, and as a voice of reason in the cacophonous Nepali political landscape. Now, for the first time, he will be tasked with rebuilding a party organization. But to do so, he will first have to dismantle the old, ossified structures and ways of thinking that have held the party back in recent times.

articles.title: Will Indonesia’s New Foreign Minister Be Allowed to Do His Job?
articles.full_text:
Arrmanatha Nasir is highly qualified, but his success may hinge on whether or not he has access to President Prabowo Subianto.
The Pancasila Building, part of the headquarters of the Indonesian Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Jakarta, Indonesia.
On October 1, Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto finally replaced Sugiono, who had served as foreign minister for the past two years, with the veteran diplomat Arrmanatha Nasir. While one may welcome the appointment of a seasoned diplomat as foreign minister, it is unclear whether he will have enough power and presidential access to steer Indonesia’s foreign policy back to a steadier, more familiar course, as under previous administrations.
As the first foreign minister in decades without substantial foreign policy experience, Sugiono’s tenure was marked by consequential decisions that broke foreign policy precedent. During his time at the helm of the Foreign Ministry, Indonesia endorsed a joint statement with China that appeared to depart from its long-standing refusal to recognize its overlapping claim with China near the Natuna Islands, potentially lending credence to China’s illegal nine-dash line claim. Additionally, it joined both BRICS and U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, and signed the unequal Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with Washington, despite this having dubious benefits to Indonesia. Internally, Indonesian diplomats made anonymous complaints to Indonesian media regarding the chaotic Foreign Ministry workflow and being left in the dark about vital foreign policy decisions that were deliberated within Prabowo’s inner circle.
In this context, Nasir’s appointment comes as a breath of fresh air. In contrast to the inexperienced Sugiono, Nasir has 29 years of experience as a Foreign Ministry insider who has filled two ambassadorial-level postings and served a five-year stint as the Ministry’s spokesperson, among other roles. Therefore, the Foreign Ministry has returned to its decades-long tradition of having career diplomats at its helm. More importantly, during his tenure as Sugiono’s vice foreign minister, Nasir was responsible for the Ministry’s internal dynamics, suggesting he should have had direct knowledge of discontent among the Ministry’s diplomats and staff. Thus, under his tenure, diplomats’ involvement in technocratic deliberations on important foreign policy matters could be improved.
While there is no doubt about Nasir’s ability to steer Indonesia’s foreign policy in the coming years, it is less clear whether he will be given the necessary opportunities and access to do so. Reports in the Indonesian news magazine Tempo indicate that access to President Prabowo, even for ministers, is very limited and heavily curated by members of his inner circle at the presidential palace, thus handicapping close coordination between the president and his cabinet members across a wide range of governmental affairs.
Foreign policy is not immune to this, and at least three major foreign policy decisions under Sugiono’s tenure were made without properly following the Foreign Ministry’s recommendations. In the lead-up to the 2024 Sino-Indonesian joint statement, Indonesian diplomats were ordered to reject any stipulation regarding joint development in overlapping areas of the South China Sea, only for the president to sign it anyway. Some reports suggest that Prabowo followed the advice of his closest confidants, who view the dispute purely in economic terms.
Additionally, high-ranking Foreign Ministry officials expressed grave concern about the one-sidedness of the U.S.-Indonesia Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed earlier this year, yet the president signed it regardless. Lastly, Indonesia joined the Board of Peace without proper deliberation with relevant Indonesian ambassadors in the Middle East, and several Indonesian diplomats anonymously complained that Indonesia’s decision to join the organization was problematic in terms of Jakarta’s policy of support for the Palestinian cause. Even Sugiono himself admitted publicly that the decision to join was made “quite fast.”
These phenomena suggest a gap in foreign policy formulation between career diplomats at the Foreign Ministry and politicians at the Presidential Palace. Ideally, the two should work in concert: Foreign Ministry staff should work out the technocratic and strategic foreign policy details, while the palace uses that advice to shape and consider broader implications beyond foreign policy, and vice versa. Additionally, bureaucrats typically spend years or decades in the Ministry, accumulating knowledge and experience that help ensure Indonesia’s foreign policy does not wildly deviate and remains consistent. If the Palace isolates itself, the views and analyses of seasoned, capable Foreign Ministry diplomats that help maintain policy stability and consistency may not be reflected in the final strategic decision, making it vulnerable to decisions of dubious benefit for Jakarta.
Nasir’s appointment, therefore, must be seen in that context. One may justifiably have little doubt about his ability to steer Indonesia’s foreign policy and muster the Ministry’s diplomats to that end. Yet, the President will have to allow the Minister quick and easy access to the Palace and ensure close coordination between it and the Ministry, such as inviting the Foreign Minister into policy deliberations with foreign policy implications and implementing his recommendations, as well as accepting the Minister’s request for an audience whenever necessary. Without proper access and consultation, no matter how brilliant or qualified the foreign minister may be, the Palace could make more major foreign policy decisions with dubious benefits and high risks.
While Prabowo wants to be more hands-on in foreign policymaking, if given access and proper consultation, an able foreign minister and diplomats can ensure that Prabowo leaves a better foreign policy legacy, since they will be able to make refined analyses and policies to achieve his goals more strategically. The question is, will the President finally muster his able foreign service to that end?
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own.

articles.title: US Drops Sanctions on Daughter of Prominent Myanmar Businessman Thein Win Zaw
articles.full_text:
Is Theint Win Htet’s removal from the Treasury Department’s blacklist a sign of a looming rapprochement between Washington and Naypyidaw?
The U.S. government has lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country’s military, after she filed two lawsuits seeking her removal from the Treasury Department’s Specially Designated Nationals List (SDN List).
According to a Reuters report, Theint Win Htet’s name was removed from the website of the Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on Friday. OFAC confirmed the deletion of her name from the SDN List in a statement the following day.
Theint Win Htet was added to the SDN List in January 2024 alongside her father Thein Win Zaw and his Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies. The Treasury Department said at the time that the company “has developed a historic relationship with Burma’s military to import and distribute petroleum,” including on behalf of Myanma Economic Holdings Public Company Limited (MEHL), a sanctioned military-linked conglomerate with tentacles in numerous sectors of Myanmar’s economy.
The listing announcement also stated that Thein Win Zaw has “provided fuel to Burma’s navy while using his companies to import petroleum and share profits with MEHL” and that he and his family members “own at least 20 companies in various sectors of the Burmese economy and are also closely associated with the regime.”
The following May, Theint Win Htet filed a lawsuit seeking her removal from the SDN List, claiming that President Joe Biden exceeded his authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act by listing the adult children of a designated individual. She also said that it had breached due process by not permitting her to contest her inclusion on the SDN List. Her case was dismissed in February 2025.
Theint Win Htet then filed a new complaint in July of this year, arguing that she has no active role in her father’s business affairs and that the sanctions had interrupted her studies in the United States. In the complaint, Reuters reported, Thein Win Htet stated that her “U.S. credit cards have been blocked, her foreign bank accounts have been restricted, closed, or refused, and she has been ​unable to complete her university studies.”
Her removal from the SDN List comes after the news agency reported that the U.S. had engaged in direct talks with the military-backed government for the first time since the February 2021 coup. According to the report, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance “joined talks” with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw on September 15-16. Numerous sources told Reuters that the talks were aimed at securing the release of detained American businessman Adam Castillo, but “also provided an opening for further engagement.”
Whether the removal of Theint Win Htet’s name is related to a possible broader diplomatic thaw remains unclear. A State Department spokesperson contacted by Reuters did not offer much explanation for the move, simply saying that the decision “reflects the administration’s determination that this designation no longer effectively supports U.S. policy objectives related to Burma.”
This is also not the first time since the coup that the name of a Myanmar individual or entity has been scrubbed from the SDN List. In July 2025, the U.S. government lifted sanctions on three Myanmar companies and a number of individuals linked to them, including KT Services & Logistics and its founder, Jonathan Myo Kyaw Thaung, who were sanctioned in 2022 for leasing Yangon’s port from MEHL. Also included on the list was Thein Win Htet’s mother Tin Latt Min.
As with last week’s announcement, OFAC did not offer a reason for the deletions, although The Irrawaddy noted that the move came after Min Aung Hlaing praised President Donald Trump in a letter responding to his threat of tariffs, in which he also commended him for shutting down U.S.-funded media outlets covering the country’s conflict. Trump administration officials said that there was “no connection between these decisions and the letter.”
Getting one’s name off the SDN List is hard even at the best of times, usually requiring the enlistment of one of a handful of specialist white shoe law firms. (Theint Win Htet was represented by Erich Ferrari, a prominent Washington-based lawyer who specializes in “economic sanctions, export controls, regulatory licensing, federal investigations, and prosecutions.”)
While the addition or removal of names from the SDN List is guided in part by legal criteria, OFAC’s decisions are often influenced by the broader policymaking climate. It is therefore plausible that a turn toward engagement with Myanmar would be accompanied by a loosening of U.S. sanctions on the country.
Whether or not this is the case here, any further shortening of the SDN List would suggest that the first steps toward engagement are evolving into a more substantial rapprochement.
