In July 2025, the U.S. government lifted sanctions on three Myanmar companies and a number of individuals linked to them, including KT Services & Logistics and its founder, Jonathan Myo Kyaw Thaung, who were sanctioned in 2022 for leasing Yangon’s port from MEHL. Also included on the list was Thein Win Htet’s mother Tin Latt Min.
As with last week’s announcement, OFAC did not offer a reason for the deletions, although The Irrawaddy noted that the move came after Min Aung Hlaing praised President Donald Trump in a letter responding to his threat of tariffs, in which he also commended him for shutting down U.S.-funded media outlets covering the country’s conflict. Trump administration officials said that there was “no connection between these decisions and the letter.”
Getting one’s name off the SDN List is hard even at the best of times, usually requiring the enlistment of one of a handful of specialist white shoe law firms. (Theint Win Htet was represented by Erich Ferrari, a prominent Washington-based lawyer who specializes in “economic sanctions, export controls, regulatory licensing, federal investigations, and prosecutions.”)
While the addition or removal of names from the SDN List is guided in part by legal criteria, OFAC’s decisions are often influenced by the broader policymaking climate. It is therefore plausible that a turn toward engagement with Myanmar would be accompanied by a loosening of U.S. sanctions on the country.
Whether or not this is the case here, any further shortening of the SDN List would suggest that the first steps toward engagement are evolving into a more substantial rapprochement.
The U.S. government has lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country’s military, after she filed two lawsuits seeking her removal from the Treasury Department’s Specially Designated Nationals List (SDN List).
According to a Reuters report, Theint Win Htet’s name was removed from the website of the Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on Friday. OFAC confirmed the deletion of her name from the SDN List in a statement the following day.
Sebastian Strangio is Southeast Asia editor at The Diplomat.
articles.summary: Is Theint Win Htet's removal from the Treasury Department's blacklist a sign of a looming rapprochement between Washington and Naypyidaw?

articles.title: Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing to Visit Indonesia and Brunei, Regime Spokesperson Says
articles.full_text:
Since taking office in April, the former general has visited five ASEAN member states as he seeks normalization with the Southeast Asian bloc.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim (right) and Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing meet at the Perdana Putra Complex in Putrajaya, Malaysia, Oct. 8, 2026.
Myanmar’s military-appointed President Min Aung Hlaing could follow up his controversial state visit to Malaysia with trips to Indonesia and Brunei, according to a Myanmar government spokesperson.
Speaking at the conclusion of Min Aung Hlaing’s two-day visit to Malaysia on Thursday, spokesperson Khaing Khaing Soe told reporters that the two nations planned to invite the Myanmar leader to make an official visit on an unspecified date. She added that Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim had shared the information with Min Aung Hlaing during their meeting in Putrajaya last week.
Malaysia was the fifth member state of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to host Min Aung Hlaing since he took office as president in April, after trips to Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. It was also the first nation from maritime Southeast Asia to host him.
The spokesperson’s comments, if confirmed, would represent just the latest diplomatic success for Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military coup of 2021. Since shedding his military fatigues and taking office as president in April, he has been on a regional charm offensive aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of much-needed foreign investment.
In addition to visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, a particular priority has been the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Since late 2021, the 11-nation bloc has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan, which called for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Since the military coup of 2021, Myanmar’s mainland Southeast Asian neighbors have been less publicly critical of the military and shown more inclination to engage the military government. The six maritime ASEAN states – Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei, and Timor-Leste – have generally been more critical and advocated a tougher regional line on Myanmar. But with a new and more legitimized government now in office in Naypyidaw, and after five years of apparently scant progress on the Five-Point Consensus, it appears that ASEAN and its member states have coalesced around a new approach.
In an interview with Singapore’s Straits Times, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who holds the rotating chairmanship of ASEAN this year, said that while the Five-Point Consensus was “absolutely correct,” the bloc needed to try a fresh approach to Myanmar.
During the bloc’s last summit in May, Marcos said, “I proposed and said we need to have a new approach on Myanmar. Nothing’s happening, so we had to do something else. And I am happy to know, because today I saw the news that the leader of Myanmar has visited Malaysia, has visited Cambodia. And that is the beginning which has never happened before.”
Whether this push towards engagement results in the full normalization of Myanmar’s relationship with ASEAN remains unclear. As Marcos’ comments suggest, the bloc has not formally abandoned the Five-Point Consensus, and there are also evidently still differences within ASEAN over how fast engagement should proceed, and to what end. While some nations, including Thailand and Malaysia, have explicitly stated that their goal is Myanmar’s eventual reintegration into ASEAN, others place more emphasis on the implementation of the Consensus.
In February, Singapore’s Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan told Parliament that the Five-Point Consensus remained the primary ASEAN reference for the Myanmar conflict, and that as such it would continue to uphold “the decision to maintain Myanmar’s non-political representation at ASEAN Summits and ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meetings,” until there is “meaningful progress” in its implementation. More recently, Singapore, which holds ASEAN’s chairmanship next year, defined this as the “permanent cessation of violence,” the release of all political detainees, and access for the ASEAN Coordinating Center for Humanitarian Assistance.
Meanwhile, Timor-Leste, which has been outspoken in its criticism of the Myanmar junta, has even permitted its legal authorities to initiate a legal case against Min Aung Hlaing and other senior officials. Indeed, Dili’s position on Myanmar may offer the first real test of whether it has been successfully socialized into the “ASEAN way.”
This suggests that even with more member states willing to roll out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing, full normalization with ASEAN, which will require a consensus among its 11 member states, will necessitate at least some gestures of compliance with the Five-Point Consensus. Myanmar military’s continued violent attacks on civilian populations, as well as its increasingly explicit rejection of the Consensus and ASEAN demands such as for an audience with detained civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, suggest that this is unlikely anytime soon.
The main question going forward, therefore, is how little ASEAN’s member states will be willing to accept in order to approve full normalization – if they don’t choose to abandon the Five-Point Consensus altogether.

articles.title: Indonesia’s Energy Investment Potential
articles.full_text:
Jakarta, Indonesia may 9 2020;Solar panels on a stand in city park, photovoltaic modules, sustainable renewable energy source.
The recent economic headlines in Indonesia have been pessimistic to say the least. There are serious concerns that President Prabowo Subianto’s signature social development initiatives – the free nutritious meals (Makanan Bergizi Gratis, “MBG) program and the Red-White Village Cooperatives (Kopdes Merah Putih) – are straining the national budget and will limit long-term growth. The president’s reluctance to abandon or significantly downsize these programs has helped inspire protests in June against an agenda which many fear is “bankrupting Indonesia.” Protestors and investors alike have additional complaints about Indonesia’s policy trajectory, including creeping militarization of the civil service, state control over key commodities sectors, and weaponization of the legal system against the government’s political opponents. Amidst the uncertainty, the rupiah and the Indonesian stock market have also experienced major slides, with the currency hitting an all-time low against the U.S. dollar on June 8 and the Jakarta Composite Index falling 36 percent from a record high in January.
Despite the serious economic headwinds, there are still opportunities for investors in the Indonesian economy, particularly in the energy sector. Indonesia ranks among global leaders in terms of energy potential and has recently improved its regulatory environment for international developers in upstream oil and gas as well as renewables. Major agreements are being signed and capital is being deployed by leading international energy companies. This momentum in domestic energy production and exploration is unfolding against the backdrop of renewed conflict in the Middle East, which has sharpened investor and policymaker focus on the risks of import dependence across the APAC region.
Recent studies have estimated that the country has technical renewable energy potential of 3,686 GW, with hundreds of suitable locations for solar, wind and hydropower facilities. To tap more of this potential, the Indonesian government has set a target energy mix of 35 percent from renewables, up from the current level of 18 percent, by 2035. However, Indonesia’s proven oil and gas reserves are also immense, totaling 2.33 billion barrels and 34.8 Tcf respectively. To utilize these reserves, Indonesia has opened 116 new oil and gas blocks to global investors.

articles.title: Indian Family Offices Eye Southeast Asia’s Startups
articles.full_text:
India’s family offices are becoming a significant force in the global economy. According to a report by The Economic Times and market intelligence firm 1Lattice, the country now hosts more than 300 family offices managing over $30 billion in assets. High-net-worth families with more than $30 million in assets are projected to nearly double, from 16,000 in 2025 to 26,000 by 2030, with intergenerational wealth transfer reaching $1.3-1.5 trillion over the next decade. A generational shift is underway as well, with over half of family offices now featuring millennials or Gen Z members in investment decisions.
The rise of younger generations has helped precipitate a change for Indian family office investment strategy: roughly 30% now favor startup allocations in healthtech, fintech, and AI, versus traditional investments such as real estate and gold. According to Tracxn data cited by CNA, family office-backed startup funding nearly doubled to $1.62 billion in 2024 from $876.7 million the year before. Analysts attribute this shift to family offices’ “patient capital” — funds without the eight-to-ten-year return pressure that constrains institutional VC — making them attractive to founders navigating longer development cycles. Cases like Sattva Group’s family office (which diversified from real estate into tech, backing firms like InCred) and Artha India Ventures (an early Oyo investor) illustrate the trend. Geopolitical volatility has reinforced the appeal of relationship-led capital, though PwC’s Falguni Shah notes governance and intrafamily alignment remain key challenges as these offices scale.
One notable growth trend among Indian family offices is the rise of impact investing, those made to achieve measurable social or environmental outcomes alongside financial returns, distinct from pure philanthropy and blended finance. Between 2021 and 2024, 923 unique HNW families made impact investments, with 86 investing through formal family office structures. Climate-tech has emerged as a leading sector, along with financial inclusion platforms and healthcare. While engagement is still early-stage and often exploratory, it signals a meaningful shift toward more value-based capital deployment among India’s wealthiest families.

articles.title: China’s Bid to Define the ‘Global South’
articles.full_text:
Beijing has adopted its own, quite different, definition of the term.
In the leadup to the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, President Xi Jinping attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, and the BRICS summit in Delhi. He also visited the Middle East — all between August and September. What is notable is that in speeches delivered at both the SCO and BRICS summits, Xi made heavy use of the term “Global South.” This reflects China’s positioning of the SCO and BRICS as gatherings of the Global South, even though Russia and Turkey are among their members. How, precisely, does China understand and deploy this term “Global South” (全球南方, Quanqiu Nanfang)?
In academic usage, “Global South” originally carried the meaning that “South” issues exist within developed countries too, and that the North-South divide should not be understood in spatially separate terms; South issues are, rather, global in character. From around 2020, however, the term began to be used differently in international forums. In particular, following the war in Ukraine, a view spread — especially in Western countries — that sharply delineated the advanced democracies against China and Russia, drawing an axis of confrontation between the developed world and China, Russia (plus Iran and North Korea), and treating the remaining countries as the “Global South.” China responded to this by becoming very wary of the term, viewing “Global South” as a Western-originated concept designed to drive a wedge between China and the developing world. China’s self-identification has been as a developing country —indeed, as the representative of the developing world. For this reason, it was unwilling to accept a term that would separate China from developing countries.
Despite this, the term “Global South” became increasingly prevalent globally. In particular, when India hosted the “Voice of Global South Summit” online on January 12 and 13, 2023, and did not invite China, this appears to have come as a significant shock to Beijing. Yet even after the “Voice of Global South Summit,” Chinese criticism of the term continued. The shift came in the period following the enactment of the Foreign Relations Law on June 28, 2023. That law, in Article 4, calls for upholding the five principles [of peaceful coexistence], and also uses the term “developing country” (发展中国家) in two places, reaffirming China’s identity as a developing country.
From July 2023, Foreign Minister Wang Yi suddenly began using the term “Global South” at international conferences, albeit with quotation marks around it. At the Meeting of BRICS National Security Advisers and High Representatives on National Security held in Johannesburg on July 25, when Wang used “Global South” in quotation marks, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning then offered a definition of the term at a press conference: “The ‘Global South’ is the family of emerging markets and developing countries.” Wang Yi listed “independence,” “development,” and “justice” as the defining qualities of the Global South, and declared that “China is a natural member of the Global South and will always be part of the developing world.” This was a definition of the Global South that clearly differed from that used in developed countries.
China has offered no explanation for this shift in approach. The most plausible interpretation is that, as the term came to be widely used globally — particularly among leaders of developing countries — and as the term’s definition remained unsettled, China made a deliberate policy shift: to define the term itself, on its own terms, and thereby shape global discourse in its favor. This too can be counted as one instance of China’s pursuit of what it calls “discourse power.”
Subsequently, not only Wang but Xi himself began using the term with quotation marks. This signaled that the term had become domestically usable within China as well. By the end of 2024, quotation marks began to be dropped from “Global South” in Chinese documents, and in a piece by Wang published in Qiushi in 2025, the quotation marks were also absent. Globally speaking, “Global South” remains a term without an agreed definition, with each actor investing it with its own meaning. China has positioned itself as a member of the Global South and has come to behave as its representative. China defines Global South as “the family of emerging markets and developing countries” — which amounts to the “non-West.” The contest over this term “Global South” throws into relief the differences in worldview between the developed world and China. The contest over this seemingly simple term, it turns out, is anything but.

There remain, to be sure, some inconsistencies in usage (instances can still be found in 2025 where Chinese officials used “Global South” with quotation marks) but these have gradually become less common, and at the SCO and BRICS meetings in 2026 cited at the outset, Xi Jinping’s use of Global South carried no quotation marks.
Globally speaking, “Global South” remains a term without an agreed definition, with each actor investing it with its own meaning. China has positioned itself as a member of the Global South and has come to behave as its representative. China defines Global South as “the family of emerging markets and developing countries” — which amounts to the “non-West.” The contest over this term “Global South” throws into relief the differences in worldview between the developed world and China. The contest over this seemingly simple term, it turns out, is anything but.
In the leadup to the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, President Xi Jinping attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, and the BRICS summit in Delhi. He also visited the Middle East — all between August and September. What is notable is that in speeches delivered at both the SCO and BRICS summits, Xi made heavy use of the term “Global South.” This reflects China’s positioning of the SCO and BRICS as gatherings of the Global South, even though Russia and Turkey are among their members. How, precisely, does China understand and deploy this term “Global South” (全球南方, Quanqiu Nanfang)?
In academic usage, “Global South” originally carried the meaning that “South” issues exist within developed countries too, and that the North-South divide should not be understood in spatially separate terms; South issues are, rather, global in character. From around 2020, however, the term began to be used differently in international forums. In particular, following the war in Ukraine, a view spread — especially in Western countries — that sharply delineated the advanced democracies against China and Russia, drawing an axis of confrontation between the developed world and China, Russia (plus Iran and North Korea), and treating the remaining countries as the “Global South.” China responded to this by becoming very wary of the term, viewing “Global South” as a Western-originated concept designed to drive a wedge between China and the developing world. China’s self-identification has been as a developing country —indeed, as the representative of the developing world. For this reason, it was unwilling to accept a term that would separate China from developing countries.
KAWASHIMA Shin is a professor at the University of Tokyo.
articles.summary: Beijing has adopted its own, quite different, definition of the term.

articles.title: Whither Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles?
articles.full_text:
A highly contentious debate is in the offing.
The U.S. Navy ballistic missile submarine USS Pennsylvania (SSBN 735) travels through the Hood Canal as it returns home following a strategic deterrence patrol Oct. 16, 2014, in Puget Sound, Wash.
Debate over the three non-nuclear principles has resurfaced in Japan as the government of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae prepares a new National Security Strategy, due at the end of 2026. Even the status of the principles is contested. Some regard them as the country’s foundational principle (kokuze), while others describe them as a policy guideline, suggesting that the government is free to change it. Prime Minister Sato Eisaku first announced the principles in 1967, and the Diet has reaffirmed them on multiple occasions since then.
The principles state that Japan will neither possess nor produce nuclear weapons, nor permit their introduction into its territory. As long as Japan remains a party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), the only practical debate concerns the third principle: non-introduction. The commitments not to possess or produce nuclear weapons nevertheless sent an important message to the world when the principles were first articulated, before Japan ratified the NPT.
In March 2010, Foreign Minister Okada Katsuya revealed that a secret agreement (mitsuyaku), broadly defined, had existed between Washington and Tokyo over the introduction of nuclear weapons. Under the U.S. interpretation, “introduction” referred only to the permanent deployment of nuclear warheads in storage facilities ashore. The Japanese government, by contrast, regarded transit through Japan’s territorial waters or port calls by nuclear-armed vessels as introduction as well. Successive Japanese leaders maintained that, in the absence of a U.S. request for “prior consultation” under the arrangements associated with the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty of 1960, Tokyo assumed that visiting U.S. vessels were not carrying nuclear weapons. Yet such vessels could not simply leave their nuclear weapons elsewhere before entering Japan. It is now an open secret that, under the Japanese definition, the United States “introduced” nuclear weapons into Japan during the Cold War.
Since the revelation in March 2010, Tokyo has maintained that there is no need to be concerned about introduction because the United States does not deploy nuclear weapons on surface vessels and has no nuclear weapon system for the vessels that regularly visit Japan. At the same time, successive Japanese governments have upheld the position Okada first articulated in the Diet that month: in extreme circumstances in which Japan’s survival cannot be secured without allowing the introduction of nuclear weapons, the government of the day “shall make a decision by taking full responsibility.” This effectively leaves open the possibility of permitting introduction in a contingency. Some therefore argue there is no need to revise the three non-nuclear principles, since they have already become “two and a half” principles.
Okada’s formula, however, does not resolve all the problems surrounding the principles. First, it only addresses contingencies, leaving unanswered how Tokyo could handle the issue in peacetime. Second, the United States is developing a nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile (SLCM-N), with the aim of making it operational in the mid-2030s. While not officially confirmed yet, the missile is expected to be carried by attack submarines of the kind that regularly visit Japan. Third, Okada’s formula addresses introduction in the Japanese sense – transit and visiting – without addressing introduction in the U.S. sense: storage ashore.
Once U.S. attack submarines begin carrying SLCM-N – or, more precisely, once they become capable of carrying it – Tokyo will find it difficult to avoid allegations that the United States is introducing nuclear weapons into Japan, regardless of whether a particular visiting submarine actually carries them. Under its longstanding “neither confirm nor deny” (NCND) policy, Washington will not disclose whether visiting submarines carry nuclear weapons. Moreover, under the U.S. definition, neither transit nor port visits constitute introduction.
This will therefore be primarily a problem for Japan. Some, particularly critics of the U.S.-Japan alliance, will argue that Tokyo should ban visits by submarines that might be carrying nuclear weapons. Doing so, however, could undermine the alliance’s deterrence and damage relations with Washington.
If Tokyo rules out denying access to U.S. submarines, it has three options. First, it could drop or amend the non-introduction principle. Second, in the most far-reaching version of such a revision, it could explicitly permit the introduction of nuclear weapons, including storage ashore as well as transit and port visits, opening the way to possible future nuclear-sharing arrangements. Third, it could adopt a narrower, more technical change: revise its definition of introduction so that transit and port visits no longer fall within it, bringing Japan’s interpretation into line with that of the United States.
Whichever option Tokyo chooses, it will be highly contentious in political terms at home. Only strong political leadership could address this problem. Many politicians appear unprepared to tackle this issue now, believing that they still have time. But it is not too early to begin laying the groundwork for a decision.

articles.title: Beyond Ideological Blocs: The ICDPP’s New Intercontinental Political Dialogue
articles.full_text:
Insights from an Interview with Chung Eui-yong on the Origins, Principles, and Future of the ICDPP
In September 2026, political leaders and party representatives from Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Europe gathered in Seoul to launch a new forum: the Inter-Continental Dialogue among Political Parties (ICDPP). Your correspondent attended the inaugural meeting as part of the CDP delegation and spoke with Chung Eui-yong about how the ICDPP emerged and the principle behind it.
The inaugural meeting brought together 23 political parties from 23 countries, including 19 governing and four opposition parties. Participants included Chung Eui-yong, chair of the Standing Committee of the International Conference of Asian Political Parties (ICAPP) and former South Korean foreign minister; Mushahid Hussain Sayed of the Pakistan Muslim League, a former information and broadcasting minister; Adem Farah Ibrahim, Ethiopia’s deputy prime minister and vice president of the ruling Prosperity Party; Milton Morrison of the Dominican Republic, vice president of the Permanent Conference of Political Parties of Latin America and the Caribbean (COPPPAL) and leader of the País Posible party; Zsolt Németh of Hungary, chair of the European Conservatives, Patriots and Affiliates group in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe; and Maiko Tajima, director of the International Department of Japan’s Constitutional Democratic Party.
The variety of political traditions represented in Seoul is central to understanding the ICDPP. This is not a forum limited to ideologically like-minded parties. Its purpose is to provide a forum in which parties with different political orientations – including governing and opposition parties – can remain in dialogue.
That principle was formally incorporated into the Seoul Declaration, unanimously adopted on September 7.
The declaration describes the ICDPP as a voluntary platform for consultation, cooperation, and confidence-building among political parties, open “irrespective of ideological orientation, governing status, or level of development.” It also stresses that the ICDPP is intended to complement, rather than replace, existing regional and international organizations.
The declaration addresses a broad range of challenges, including geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, climate change, economic uncertainty, technological transformation, and inequality. Participants reaffirmed their commitment to the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter, international law, human rights, the rule of law, sustainable development, and multilateral cooperation. They also agreed to continue ICDPP meetings and develop institutional arrangements and future work programs.
Its concluding phrase summarized the aspiration behind the new forum: “dialogue over dispute, cooperation over confrontation, and partnership over polarization.”
The ICDPP did not emerge suddenly. It builds on more than two decades of political party dialogue developed through the ICAPP and its regional partners. The ICAPP was founded in 2000 at the initiative of former Philippine House Speaker Jose de Venecia Jr. Chung, who became involved after entering South Korean politics in 2004, later played an important role in its institutional development, including drafting the ICAPP Charter and helping establish its Standing Committee and regular meetings.
In addition to this institutional development, the ICAPP gradually expanded its dialogue beyond Asia. It established regular exchanges with the Permanent Conference of Political Parties of Latin America and the Caribbean (COPPPAL), developed the Asia-Europe Political Forum with European political groups, and promoted contacts with African political parties. The establishment in Ghana in 2025 of the African Political Parties Initiative (APPI) added a new institutional partner in Africa.
With ties established across the Americas, Europe, and Africa, Chung explained: “I thought it’s about time” to hold a meeting involving the four regions. He proposed the name “Inter-Continental Dialogue among Political Parties,” and the idea received support from the regional partners.
The ICDPP can therefore be understood as the culmination of a gradual process: regional political party dialogue in Asia expanding into cross-regional dialogue and, eventually, an intercontinental framework.
The principle inherited from the ICAPP is as important as the network itself. The ICAPP developed as a forum open to political parties from different ideological traditions, rather than one organized around a single political family. Chung incorporated that principle into the ICAPP Charter when the organization was being institutionalized.
Asked why, Chung replied: “I tell you my conviction. Why should we be divided by ideological orientation? And why can’t we talk to each other?”
He explained that he had held the same view in domestic politics. When Chung entered politics in 2004, some in his own Democratic Party were skeptical of bipartisan diplomacy, while persuading the conservative opposition to cooperate was not easy. Today, however, South Korea’s major rival parties cooperate in ICAPP activities.
The same thinking is visible in the Seoul Declaration. It describes differences in political traditions and cultures not simply as obstacles, but as possible sources of “strength and mutual learning.” This does not mean that the ICDPP expects political disagreements to disappear. On the contrary, disagreement is built into the design of the forum.
At the welcome dinner on the eve of the inaugural meeting, Chung told delegates that they should not expect everyone around the table to think alike.
“Our political traditions, experiences, and perspectives are different,” he said. Those differences, he continued, should be acknowledged and respected. The aim was to create a space in which they could be discussed openly and constructively, while keeping channels of communication open – especially “when circumstances become difficult and dialogue is needed most.”
That may be the clearest expression of what distinguishes the ICDPP. Its purpose is not to create ideological unity, but to sustain political communication despite ideological difference.
The challenge now is whether that dialogue can produce results. A forum encompassing parties with widely different political traditions and geopolitical interests may find it relatively easy to meet, but much harder to reach common positions or act collectively.
Chung himself raised precisely this issue in his opening remarks. “The significance of this initiative,” he said, should not be measured simply by the number or diversity of participants around the table, but by the ability to “build sustained dialogue and turn our conversations into meaningful action.”
The Seoul Declaration provides the first steps: regular meetings, further discussions on rules and institutional arrangements, future work programs, and broader participation while retaining the voluntary and inclusive character of the forum.
Whether the ICDPP will develop into an effective mechanism for cooperation remains an open question. Its significance will ultimately depend not on the number of parties represented at future meetings, but on whether relationships built through repeated dialogue can survive periods of political tension – and whether those relationships can contribute to practical cooperation on common challenges.
At the welcome dinner in Seoul, Chung described what he hoped the gathering might eventually become: a community of political leaders who made a deliberate choice to continue talking, listening, and working together across continents, “even when our views are different.”

articles.title: Why Afghanistan’s Neighbors Have Not Backed Pakistan’s Strikes on the Taliban
articles.full_text:
China, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan are less exposed to the impact of cross-border terrorism – and less willing to risk smooth relations with Kabul over the issue.
The eighth meeting of the Moscow Format consultations on Afghanistan in Moscow, Russia, Oct. 5, 2026.
On October 5, Moscow hosted the eighth meeting of the special representatives and senior officials from regional countries for the Moscow Format to discuss political and economic relations with Afghanistan and counterterrorism and counter-narcotics cooperation. The Moscow Format includes Afghanistan, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan.
But the meeting failed to adopt a joint statement because the Pakistani and Afghan delegates disagreed over the language on terrorism. The Taliban objected to the frequent mention of terrorism in reference to Afghanistan. 
Russia’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, said the Afghan delegates accepted similar language last year. He believed that the changed relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan might have caused Kabul’s objection this time.
The meeting was held only a week after the most recent confrontation between Islamabad and Kabul. On September 18 and 26, Pakistan suffered deadly terrorist attacks in its northwestern province, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, that together killed about 44 people and injured about 138. Pakistan responded with airstrikes on different targets in Afghanistan that it believes were the training camps and hideouts of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and its associated factions responsible for the cross-border attacks.
At the Moscow summit, Pakistan’s delegation said the Taliban were complicit in those attacks in Pakistan because the terrorist groups were operating on Afghan soil with impunity. The Taliban said Pakistan was using military aggression in violation of international law for an issue that could be resolved through political negotiations.
The Moscow Format meeting failed to bridge these differences enough to allow for a joint communique. What’s noteworthy is that other countries that share borders with Afghanistan – such as China, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – did not use their diplomatic capital to reach an understanding on language that included everyone’s concerns.
Afghanistan’s neighbors have different levels of concern about militancy there. Their strategies, especially on counterterrorism, are a function of the nature of their border with Afghanistan, the extent of the threat from militant groups on Afghan soil, and the Taliban’s scale of cooperation regarding those groups. From their perspective, military force is not the most effective solution to address the issue.
China shares a border of only about 92 kilometers with Afghanistan, high in the Wakhan Corridor, marked by rough terrain and the nearly 5,000-meter high Wakhjir Pass. In terms of a terrorist presence in Afghanistan, Beijing considers the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) its main concern and has pressed the Taliban to act against the group. The Taliban have reportedly relocated ETIM fighters away from the border, and they now have a dispersed presence. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat to China is smaller, and any movement across the pass is easy to detect. 
Uzbekistan similarly shares a short border of 144 kilometers with Afghanistan, almost entirely along the Amu Darya. Regular cross-border movement is concentrated at the closely guarded Termez-Hairatan road and rail crossing. But the militant groups in Afghanistan that concern Tashkent have shown only a limited capacity for cross-border attacks. There was one incident in 2022 of rockets being fired toward Termez, which didn’t cause any casualties. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat is relatively small and easier to contain.
Tajikistan’s case is closer to Pakistan’s in terms of the long border and threat. Dushanbe shares about 1,374 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, much of which runs along the Panj River and passes through remote and mountainous territory and is difficult to monitor consistently. The cross-border threat therefore needs more immediate attention. In November 2025, two cross-border attacks from Afghanistan’s Badakhshan province killed five Chinese workers in Tajikistan. 
As for Taliban cooperation, Kabul has offered these countries help in investigations and has arrested suspects after cross-border attacks. 
Pakistan’s case is of a different magnitude on all these counts. 
Pakistan shares 2,640 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, where Pashtun and Baloch communities live on both sides. Afghanistan has never recognized the border since Pakistan’s founding. Islamabad has been fencing it since 2017, but militants continue to cross it. A disputed frontier with kinship networks on both sides gives militants far more routes and tricks to enter Pakistan than Afghanistan’s northern borders offer. 
Pakistan also faces a much larger threat. Its key concerns are the TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), and the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). Islamabad charges that all three groups have a presence in Afghanistan, especially the TTP. U.N. monitors estimate the TTP, which has carried out the most frequent and lethal attacks in Pakistan, has about 6,000 fighters in Afghanistan. 
By September 2026, Pakistan’s terrorism situation had worsened sharply, with 1,232 militant attacks in nine months, already 169 attacks above those recorded in all of 2025. Consistent attacks on this scale raise domestic pressure to take firm action.
Moreover, the Taliban have shown limited willingness to cooperate with Pakistan on the issue of militant groups. The Taliban leadership describes TTP members as Pakistani refugees and refuses to classify them as militants. U.N. monitors report that the group enjoys greater liberty and support from Taliban authorities. Kabul has offered to relocate the TTP fighters away from the Pakistani border, but that step cannot stop the militant movement through the long and porous border with Pakistan. 
Pakistan has, therefore, asked for written guarantees that the militants would not use Afghan soil as a base for attacks in Pakistan. The Taliban have rejected this demand, which was why the Istanbul talks failed in November 2025.
Pakistan has said its operations will continue until the Taliban take verifiable action against militant groups on Afghan soil. Yet none of Afghanistan’s neighbors has publicly supported Pakistan’s airstrikes. China, Russia, and Iran have called for restraint and offered to mediate, and Uzbekistan urged a diplomatic resolution. China hosted informal talks in Urumqi in April but those ended without agreement. 
Whether in Urumqi or more recently in Moscow, repeated efforts at finding common ground have fallen flat. While none of Afghanistan’s neighbors is comfortable with the idea of cross-border terrorism, none of them has sanctioned Pakistan’s military retaliation, either.
