articles.title: What Pakistan Will and Won’t Do in Yemen
articles.full_text:
Operationally, it would make little sense for Pakistan to send in large conventional ground forces to Yemen simply to put the brakes on Houthi advances.
Turkish President Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohamed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif hold copies of the Mecca Agreement after its signing on August 7, 2026.
On October 5, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan moved ahead to activate their defense commitments and provide military capabilities agreed under the Mecca Defense Alliance. The decision came after weeks of Houthi drone and missile strikes against Saudi Arabia, even as the Houthis were ramping up their ground operations along the Red Sea coast.
Regardless of how the crisis plays out, the Houthi conflict has turned out to be the first major test of the Mecca Pact. The alliance must strike a balance. It has to demonstrate that its commitments have real military value without crossing the line into becoming an interventionist force or getting bogged down in a prolonged war of attrition.
For Pakistan, the Houthi crisis is a particularly difficult strategic problem.
There is broad agreement within Pakistan’s strategic community that the Mecca Pact is defensive rather than offensive. However, Pakistan cannot simply sit on the sidelines as the regional security environment goes downhill and its own defensive commitments come under strain. If the alliance cannot show up when one of its members faces a serious security challenge, its deterrent value could quickly erode.
At the same time, Pakistan is alive to the costs of direct intervention. Deploying large numbers of troops into Yemen would pile on additional pressure on an already stretched military, which is grappling with counterterrorism challenges at home and the threat from India. It could also put a strain on its relations with Iran and, perhaps most importantly, lock Islamabad into a commitment from which it would find it difficult to pull out without paying a heavy strategic price.
Diplomatically, Islamabad is trying to persuade Iran into restraining the Houthis. Nonetheless, there are limits to what Tehran can or is willing to do. Iranian influence over Houthi decision-making is significant but is not unlimited. The Houthis have an axe to grind when it comes to Saudi Arabia. Moreover, Tehran has little obvious incentive to do away with a source of pressure on Saudi Arabia while it is itself preparing for another round with the United States. Therefore, diplomacy is unlikely to resolve the crisis on its own.
Pakistan must demonstrate that the Mecca Pact has real teeth and practical military value. To understand what that support might look like, it is necessary to understand the alliance’s objectives and the means available to achieve them.
Pakistan understands that wiping out the Houthis altogether is neither realistic nor desirable. Even if such an objective were militarily achievable, the costs would be high. Sustained Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, combined with the consequences of further stoking Yemen’s civil war, could make the price of total military victory prohibitively high.
The more realistic objective, therefore, is to constrain the Houthis’ ability to dominate the Bab al-Mandeb and tip the military balance sufficiently to open up space for a political settlement.
Any military support that Pakistan or Türkiye provides to Saudi Arabia or Saudi-backed forces in Yemen should be understood in this light.
Operationally, it would make little sense for Pakistan to send in large conventional ground forces to Yemen simply to put the brakes on Houthi advances. The decisive fighting is taking place in southwestern Yemen, particularly around Taiz and Mocha. These areas are far from the Saudi border. Operating a large Pakistani expeditionary force there would be logistically difficult and risky.
What is needed instead is a capable and better-organized anti-Houthi force in southwestern Yemen. This is where Pakistan and Türkiye can add value. Both countries can supply weapons and other military assistance to Saudi-backed forces, beefing up their ability to conduct counteroffensives. They can also help with command-and-control structures, where weaknesses have contributed to the inability of anti-Houthi forces to push back against recent Houthi advances.
Pakistan also has extensive experience with special operations and counterterrorism, particularly from its campaigns in Afghanistan. Türkiye, meanwhile, has built up considerable experience operating specialized forces in Syria and Iraq. Therefore, both could provide specialized personnel and advisers potentially inside Yemen without committing to large conventional formations. In this sense, Pakistan and Türkiye could contribute through force augmentation rather than direct intervention.
Another potential priority would be breaking up Houthi command structures. The Houthis have become more organized and militarily sophisticated, but they still retain many characteristics of a networked armed movement. Weakening their command and communications could pay off more than attempting to wear down the organization through conventional territorial warfare alone. Pakistan and Türkiye’s intelligence-gathering experience could offer useful lessons for Saudi Arabia and its local partners in this regard.
The alliance must also brace for further attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. Saudi Arabia’s air-defense network could come under increasing pressure if Houthi missile and drone attacks intensify. Already, Saudi air-defense stockpiles are thinned due to Iranian attacks and continued Houthi onslaughts. Therefore, Pakistan and Türkiye would provide additional air-defense capabilities and personnel to shield critical infrastructure and strategic facilities.
Saudi Arabia already has a substantial air force and does not necessarily require Pakistani fighter aircraft or pilots. What it needs more urgently is support in battlefield operational planning, target identification and air-combat support functions. Such assistance could improve both the effectiveness and intensity of Saudi air operations.
This broader role explains why deployment of as many as 40,000 Pakistani troops should not be read as preparation for a conventional Pakistani ground war in Yemen.
Nonetheless, there are limits to what Pakistan can pull off. The operationalization of the Mecca Pact’s joint command remains in its infancy. Moreover, it is unclear how effectively Pakistan’s military capabilities can be integrated into a conflict with a very different geography and political environment. Pakistan also has considerably less experience in indirectly shaping a battlefield by strengthening another state’s forces.
There is another uncertainty. The strategic objectives of Pakistan and Saudi Arabia may not stay in lockstep as the conflict evolves. Riyadh may ultimately seek to tip the balance of power in Yemen decisively in its favor. Islamabad, by contrast, is likely to remain committed to its defense obligations while seeking to steer clear of a prolonged military commitment. The two countries’ objectives may overlap during the initial phase of the crisis, but they could diverge as the conflict drags on.
A far more serious crisis could flare up if Iran or its allies in Iraq move to support the Houthis. Iraqi militias have already attacked Saudi Arabia several times, including strikes on the East-West Crude Oil Pipeline. While Iran’s direct intervention remains off the table for the moment, the situation would change if the US resumes massive strikes on Iran, including on energy infrastructure. Iran will surely hit back at Gulf energy infrastructure, Saudi Arabia’s included. The conflict would then spill over beyond Yemen.
How the Mecca Defense Alliance manages the Houthi crisis will shape not only the integrity of the Mecca Pact but also its credibility as a foundation for the emerging regional security order.

articles.title: A Raid on a Gay Bar Risks Taiwan’s LGBTQ-Friendly Reputation
articles.full_text:
An attorney says authorities overstepped legal bounds, and activists warn of discrimination ahead of Asia’s largest Pride event.
A rainbow crosswalk in Ximending, Taipei, Taiwan.
A patron at a well-known gay bar in Taipei recalls being “extremely shocked and confused” when around 30 police staged a dramatic raid on October 3 and took dozens of people away for questioning.
The raid occurred just four weeks before Taipei’s annual Pride celebration. Footage of officers using demeaning language and what attorneys have described as unlawful treatment spurred an estimated 100 protesters to march on precinct headquarters the next day.
While several officers have been disciplined, LGBTQ+ advocates say the issue goes beyond the actions of a few. They are calling for structural changes to protect the rights of sexual minorities in a city that has come to be known for tolerance.
“This incident exposes a serious gap. A city can celebrate LGBTQ+ communities publicly but still not ensure everyone is treated equally by institutions like the police,” Sean Du, secretary-general of the Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association, Taiwan’s largest LGBTQ+ advocacy group, said.
Taiwan has built a reputation as one of Asia’s most LGBTQ+-friendly societies in the decades since the police crackdowns and harassment of the martial law era that ended in 1987.
Taiwan became the first in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage in 2019. For queer travelers from countries in the region where same-sex relations are stigmatized or even criminalized, Taipei has become something of a liberal bastion. The island also boasts Asia’s largest Pride parade, held annually on the last Saturday of October, with an estimated 150,000 attending last year.
The raid targeted Commander D, a 14-year-old BDSM-themed club in Wanhua District’s Ximending area. Wanhua Precinct police said they had received 13 complaints about Commander D from members of the public between January 1 and Saturday, October 3.
Police visits are not unusual at Taipei clubs; officers typically check IDs before heading on their way. But this time officers came armed with a search warrant approved by the Taipei District Court.
Lin, 34, a clinical psychologist and founder of the independent Threads publication Taipei Rainbow Party Weekly, said he had witnessed numerous nightclub inspections before but that Saturday’s was a “fundamentally different” encounter, one that left some of his friends traumatized.
More than 30 police, including uniformed and plainclothes officers, flooded Commander D at around 4:30 p.m., stopping the music and turning on the lights, Lin said. Videos shared on social media by others showed officers ordering customers to squat down and put away their phones.
Police told the media they had found used condoms and that some customers were nude. Those not wearing clothes were not allowed to put them back on, while those who had hastily gotten dressed were made to remove their clothes to preserve evidence, Lin recounted.
Of the 58 customers police say were inside, around two-thirds were shirtless and most of the rest in their underwear. Only a few were completely naked, Lin said.
Police did not initially display the warrant to those gathered, witnesses said. A video shared on social media shows police repeatedly ordering customers to stop talking, telling them to challenge the operation in court. 
Officers also mocked a man for being in a wheelchair, questioning whether he was able to have sex. When a manager came to the man’s defense, he was handcuffed and made to kneel on the floor, local media cited eyewitnesses as saying.
Patrons had their belongings searched and were subjected to a urine test for drugs. After several hours, 51 people were loaded into police vehicles and taken to the precinct for further questioning as “witnesses.” 
Commander D did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Several police actions that day were legally problematic, according to Lingwei Li, founder and managing lawyer at Zenkuan Law Firm and founder of the Taiwan Nonbinary Queer Sluts, Taiwan’s first support group for nonbinary people.
A warrant to search the premises does not automatically entitle police to search every customer’s property, and individual searches require separate criteria or consent, Li said.
Compulsory drug tests, meanwhile, should be limited to persons placed under arrest, not witnesses. Li told The Diplomat they were not aware of any legal basis for barring witnesses from using their phones.
Police also blurred the line between a witness and a suspect, Li said. A witness cannot simply be detained unless they fail to appear without good reason after being formally summoned to testify and a warrant has then been issued.
Addressing the question of nudity, Li said the Social Order Maintenance Act requires more than mere nudity to qualify as an offense, including conduct that offends public decency and continues despite a warning. “This case involves an abuse of police authority,” Li said. “Evidence indicates that the police prohibited the nude individual from putting on clothes, which also contradicts the requirement of ‘failing to heed warnings.’”
“Ordering people who were already dressed to undress is not preserving evidence. It’s humiliation.”
Wanhua Precinct’s investigation found four officers had used inappropriate language. “They have been dealt with strictly,” the precinct told The Diplomat. Each received two reprimands. The official who supervised the operation received a demerit, while the precinct chief himself was issued two reprimands after voluntarily requesting disciplinary action.
“The precinct respects diverse communities and will undertake a thorough review of officers’ on-site enforcement procedures,” the statement said. “It will comprehensively strengthen education and training and require officers, when carrying out their duties in the future, to continue to respect the cultures of a diverse society, in order to safeguard residents’ rights and interests and prevent similar controversies from occurring again.”
No charges have been filed yet in connection with the raid. In a separate statement, police said Commander D’s owner, surnamed Zhong, 44, was referred to the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office on suspicion of violating public decency, according to a press statement viewed by the Central News Agency.
Commander D had been in the news before. During a September 11 session at the Taipei City Council, Councilor Hung Chien-yi repeated a parent’s claim that minors were entering bars and displayed photos of a venue media identified as Commander D. 
The club denied these claims and insisted its staff check IDs before allowing patrons to enter. It’s not clear if those allegations were related to the raid last week.
On October 7, a civil society group filed a criminal complaint with the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office over alleged police misconduct during the raid, the precinct told the Diplomat. The police said the matter was now subject to investigative confidentiality.
articles.summary: An attorney says authorities overstepped legal bounds, and activists warn of discrimination ahead of Asia's largest Pride event.

articles.title: The Bangsamoro’s New Government Faces a Test of Public Trust
articles.full_text:
The main challenge of the incoming administration will be to sustain the peace process with Manila while representing the interests of local residents.
The parliament of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in Cotabato City, Philippines.
Last month’s parliamentary election in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines, the first ever, has settled one question but opened another.
The election results are now clear. The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) secured 31 seats across the party and district races, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) 30, and the BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC) 15, with the remaining seats going to other parties and sectoral representatives. No party has the 41 votes needed to elect the chief minister. The 80 elected members of the first regular Parliament are set to assume office on October 30, marking the formal transition from the interim government to the first elected Bangsamoro government.
Most attention has understandably been directed at the question of which parties might come together to form the “Government of the Day”. But whatever its composition, the coalition that eventually emerges will offer an early indication of what kind of political order is taking shape in the Bangsamoro.
The September 14 election marked a transitional milestone from a negotiated peace settlement to elected government. The election results bring together political forces with different origins. BFP is composed of former combatants of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), including local political figures. The UBJP is associated with the MILF, while BGC brings together established political parties and clan-based political networks.
The poll also reflects the changing place of the Moro National Liberation Front,  a Moro armed movement that signed a separate peace agreement with the Philippine government in 1996, in this political order. Its two political parties from its two major factions – the Mahardika and the Bangsamoro Party – did not secure seats as Sulu, where the MNLF has historically had a strong political presence, is no longer part of the BARMM electorate. But MNLF-linked voices have entered the new political order through other parties and individual representatives.
For the BFP, its coalition choice means defining what its break from the UBJP political camp means for the next phase of Bangsamoro politics. A BFP-UBJP alliance would bring together the two largest parties, potentially forming the “super majority”. The two share roots in the broader MILF political tradition but have since taken different political paths, particularly after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Abdulraof Macacua,  then chief of staff of the MILF’s armed wing,  the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces, as BARMM’s interim chief minister in 2025.   Macacua later joined BFP and became its chair and president.
Such a coalition would test whether political differences within the former movement can be managed within the institutions created by the peace process.  It could also allow BFP to broaden its political base through UBJP’s strong showing in the sectoral races, while bringing BFP’s relationship with Manila into a broader governing coalition.
For UBJP, a BFP coalition would likewise have significant implications. The party remains closely associated with the MILF and the peace agreement that produced the BARMM. An UBJP-BFP coalition could provide continuity with this political project within the new parliamentary system. BFP’s perceived close relationship with Malacañang could help move some of the remaining normalization commitments. At the same time, such a coalition would require UBJP to navigate the question of national government influence, which has contributed to political divisions within the MILF.
For a Bangsamoro public that has long been sensitive to Manila’s role in BARMM governance, the stakes would extend beyond securing a parliamentary majority.  The two political strands that emerged from the MILF would have to work together without blurring the distinction between cooperation with the national government in implementing the peace process and preserving political autonomy for the Bangsamoro.
The BGC faces a different choice. With 15 seats, it has the numbers needed by either BFP or UBJP to form a majority. It has already indicated that it is open to working with either party, and its political forces bring established parties, local networks, and experience in governing into an arena increasingly shaped by MILF-linked politics. As such, it could bring familiarity with local government and the political relationships and practices that have shaped the region for decades. At the same time, its ranks include emerging political voices who may bring different priorities and forms of representation to the new Parliament. Depending on its choice, the BGC’s role in shaping the first elected government could either reinforce established ways of exercising political power or broaden what the new parliamentary system can represent.
BFP has since announced that it has secured enough support to form a majority, although coalition discussions among the parties are continuing. This makes the coalition combinations less hypothetical. A BFP-UBJP coalition signals an effort to reconcile competing strands of the MILF political project. A BFP-BGC or UBJP-BGC coalition would demonstrate how movement-linked politics and established political networks are negotiating power within the new parliamentary system. Much will depend on what the parties ask of one another in exchange for governing together and what they are prepared to commit to the Bangsamoro public. But the burden now falls more heavily on BFP to show what this majority is assembled around. Securing votes is one task; building a coalition with a shared governing agenda is another. A coalition can be politically viable without necessarily being ideologically coherent.
If the BGC and the established political networks aligned with it are central to the new government, that would not necessarily mean a reversal of the political transformation envisioned by the peace process. It could instead show that the new political order is becoming a negotiated space between movement-linked politics and longstanding sources of local political power.
However, the coalition question cannot be separated from the environment in which the new government will have to govern. As I noted before the polls, the challenge was not simply avoiding localized violence but ensuring that political disputes could still be contained through the institutions and relationships established by the peace process.
In Cotabato City, election-related violence before and on election day left several people dead and injured. Shortly after the election, localized fighting in BARMM’s Special Geographic Area prompted the deployment of joint Philippine government-MILF security mechanisms. These incidents exposed the complexity of the transition currently taking place in BARMM.
Another issue that may become more visible is the relationship between the new Bangsamoro government and Manila. With an elected government taking shape, the Bangsamoro public has stronger expectations that the BARMM should have greater political space to determine its leadership and governing arrangements. The issue will be how Manila’s involvement is perceived: as a support for Bangsamoro institutions or as an attempt to shape their political outcomes. If the latter perception takes hold, it could complicate the new government’s efforts to establish its own political authority.
For the incoming government, the mandate should extend beyond running the regional administration. It will also have to demonstrate a clear commitment to completing the remaining normalization commitments under the peace process, working closely with the MILF as a peace partner while maintaining a constructive relationship with the national government – while not becoming so closely identified with either that it loses the political space needed to govern in the interests of the Bangsamoro people.
The peace process in the southern Philippines sought to create institutions through which political authority could be acquired, exercised, and contested. The challenge for the new government will be to remain autonomous enough to govern in the interests of local people, but engaged enough to sustain the peace process.

No party has the 41 votes needed to elect the chief minister. The 80 elected members of the first regular Parliament are set to assume office on October 30, marking the formal transition from the interim government to the first elected Bangsamoro government.
Most attention has understandably been directed at the question of which parties might come together to form the “Government of the Day”. But whatever its composition, the coalition that eventually emerges will offer an early indication of what kind of political order is taking shape in the Bangsamoro.
The September 14 election marked a transitional milestone from a negotiated peace settlement to elected government. The election results bring together political forces with different origins. BFP is composed of former combatants of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), including local political figures. The UBJP is associated with the MILF, while BGC brings together established political parties and clan-based political networks.
The poll also reflects the changing place of the Moro National Liberation Front,  a Moro armed movement that signed a separate peace agreement with the Philippine government in 1996, in this political order. Its two political parties from its two major factions – the Mahardika and the Bangsamoro Party – did not secure seats as Sulu, where the MNLF has historically had a strong political presence, is no longer part of the BARMM electorate. But MNLF-linked voices have entered the new political order through other parties and individual representatives.
For the BFP, its coalition choice means defining what its break from the UBJP political camp means for the next phase of Bangsamoro politics. A BFP-UBJP alliance would bring together the two largest parties, potentially forming the “super majority”. The two share roots in the broader MILF political tradition but have since taken different political paths, particularly after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Abdulraof Macacua,  then chief of staff of the MILF’s armed wing,  the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces, as BARMM’s interim chief minister in 2025.   Macacua later joined BFP and became its chair and president.
Such a coalition would test whether political differences within the former movement can be managed within the institutions created by the peace process.  It could also allow BFP to broaden its political base through UBJP’s strong showing in the sectoral races, while bringing BFP’s relationship with Manila into a broader governing coalition.
For UBJP, a BFP coalition would likewise have significant implications. The party remains closely associated with the MILF and the peace agreement that produced the BARMM. An UBJP-BFP coalition could provide continuity with this political project within the new parliamentary system. BFP’s perceived close relationship with Malacañang could help move some of the remaining normalization commitments. At the same time, such a coalition would require UBJP to navigate the question of national government influence, which has contributed to political divisions within the MILF.
For a Bangsamoro public that has long been sensitive to Manila’s role in BARMM governance, the stakes would extend beyond securing a parliamentary majority.  The two political strands that emerged from the MILF would have to work together without blurring the distinction between cooperation with the national government in implementing the peace process and preserving political autonomy for the Bangsamoro.
The BGC faces a different choice. With 15 seats, it has the numbers needed by either BFP or UBJP to form a majority. It has already indicated that it is open to working with either party, and its political forces bring established parties, local networks, and experience in governing into an arena increasingly shaped by MILF-linked politics. As such, it could bring familiarity with local government and the political relationships and practices that have shaped the region for decades. At the same time, its ranks include emerging political voices who may bring different priorities and forms of representation to the new Parliament. Depending on its choice, the BGC’s role in shaping the first elected government could either reinforce established ways of exercising political power or broaden what the new parliamentary system can represent.
BFP has since announced that it has secured enough support to form a majority, although coalition discussions among the parties are continuing. This makes the coalition combinations less hypothetical. A BFP-UBJP coalition signals an effort to reconcile competing strands of the MILF political project. A BFP-BGC or UBJP-BGC coalition would demonstrate how movement-linked politics and established political networks are negotiating power within the new parliamentary system. Much will depend on what the parties ask of one another in exchange for governing together and what they are prepared to commit to the Bangsamoro public. But the burden now falls more heavily on BFP to show what this majority is assembled around. Securing votes is one task; building a coalition with a shared governing agenda is another. A coalition can be politically viable without necessarily being ideologically coherent.
articles.summary: The main challenge of the incoming administration will be to sustain the peace process with Manila while representing the interests of local residents.

articles.title: Former Philippine President Duterte Fit to Stand Trial, ICC Says
articles.full_text:
An independent panel of experts said that the 81-year-old “has the capacity to understand the charges” and “the purpose and consequences” of the trial proceedings.
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte attends a status conference at Trial Chamber III of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands, Sep. 16, 2026.
Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have ruled ‌that former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is fit to stand trial on charges linked to his violent “war on drugs.”
The ruling by Trial Chamber III, which was made on September 28 but only made public yesterday, was “based on the findings of an independent Panel of Experts as well as on submissions made by the parties and participants on these issues,” the ICC said in a statement.
“The Expert Panel unanimously found that the Accused has the capacity to understand the charges, understand the purpose and consequences of the proceedings, follow the course of the proceedings, including the nature and implications of entering a plea, understand the evidence, and instruct counsel in the preparation and conduct of his defense,” it said.
Duterte, 81, is set to go on trial on November 30, and faces three charges of crimes against humanity for extrajudicial killings carried out during the anti-drug campaign, a flagship policy of his administration between 2016 and 2022.
Duterte’s attorneys claimed last year that he was in frail health and that his condition was deteriorating in the ICC’s detention unit. In one filing in June, they argued that the ex-president’s illness and “advanced age” created “compelling humanitarian grounds” for judges to grant his interim release. In January, judges rejected the defense claims, arguing that Duterte “is able effectively to exercise his procedural rights and is therefore fit to take part in the pre-trial proceedings.”
The September 28 ruling comes in response to a separate petition, submitted in September 2025, in which Duterte’s lawyers claimed that he was unfit to stand trial due to “cognitive impairment in multiple domains.”
The former leader has been in the court’s custody since his arrest in the Philippines in March 2025. In April, the ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed the charges against Duterte and ordered the case to go to trial. The chamber’s judges concluded that “there are substantial grounds to believe that Mr. Duterte is responsible for the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder.” These crimes “were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population on the territory of the Republic of the Philippines.”
Specifically, Duterte is charged with the murders of at least ⁠76 people and the attempted murder of two ​others. Nineteen of the alleged murders were carried out between 2013 and 2016, when Duterte was mayor of Davao City. The remainder were committed during the “war on drugs” campaign, which Duterte launched upon becoming president in 2016. The campaign resulted in a death toll of at least 6,000 – the official estimate of the Philippine police – but independent estimates run as high as 30,000.
However, during an in-person appearance at the ICC last month, Duterte was thin and haggard, suggesting that questions about his health and advanced age will continue to hang over his trial. With this in mind, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner at a status conference last month expressed concerns about the volume of evidence in the case against Duterte and the length of the prosecution case. She said the chamber was “very anxious” that the prosecution case should conclude “as swiftly as possible in the circumstances,” so that Duterte lives to see a verdict.

articles.title: US Has Opened Direct Talks With Myanmar Government, Report Claims
articles.full_text:
The outreach, which marks a significant shift in U.S. policy, is aimed at curbing online scamming operations and gaining access to the country’s rare earth deposits.
The plaza of the Uppatasanti Pagoda in Naypyidaw, Myanmar, at sunset.
Yesterday, Reuters published a report stating that the Trump administration has begun direct talks with Myanmar’s military-installed government for the first time since the 2021 coup, marking a significant change in U.S. policy toward the country.
According to the report, which was authored by Reuters’ Simon Lewis and cited seven current and former U.S. officials and others familiar with the ‌policy shift, this engagement has so far focused on discreet issues, such as efforts to shut down the online scam centers, but “could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits.”
The report claimed that U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance “joined talks” with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw on September 15-16. The meeting was nominally aimed at securing the release of detained American businessman Adam Castillo, but also provided an opening for further engagement, four of the sources told Reuters.
Whether or not it is sustained, the engagement marks an important shift in U.S. policy towards Myanmar. When Min Aung Hlaing seized power in a coup in 2021, terminating a decade of political and economic reforms, the U.S. government quickly reimposed economic sanctions on senior generals and businesses linked to the military. The following year, it downgraded its diplomatic representation in the country, reverting to the policy that pertained between 1987 and 2012, when the U.S. was represented by a chief of mission rather than a fully credentialed ambassador.
The Reuters report also identified how Myanmar’s new military government used the detention of Castillo, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar who was arrested at Yangon airport in June on opaque charges, in order to advance diplomatic re-engagement with Washington.
The September meeting between Vance and Min Aung Hlaing was preceded by back-channel negotiations between U.S. and Myanmar officials aimed at securing Castillo’s release. During these talks, Reuters reported, Myanmar “only asked for an official engagement at the right level with the U.S. government” in return.
The report makes clear that these were not the first engagements between U.S. and Myanmar officials. In June, the two sides held meetings in Tokyo; one source cited by the news agency said that in addition to Vance, “officials from the Treasury Department, which oversees sanctions, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Pentagon took part.” Josh Kurlantzick of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) wrote yesterday that several sources had also told him that prior to Vance’s visit to Naypyidaw, “U.S. officials had been secretly meeting with officials from Myanmar in Japan.”
The purpose of this engagement, the Reuters report states, was to combat the online scamming operations that have become deeply rooted in Myanmar since the coup, and which have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars. It added that “U.S. officials also discussed access to Myanmar’s massive ​deposits of heavy rare earths,” most of which are located in areas of northern Myanmar currently under the control of rebel forces including the Kachin Independence Army (KIA).
Myanmar’s rare earth deposits have gradually become something of an idée fixe for certain elements of the Trump administration, as it seeks to reduce its heavy reliance on China, which controls a large part of the world’s supply of these critical minerals.
In July 2025, Reuters reported that administration officials had “heard competing proposals” for changes to U.S. policy aimed at gaining access to the rare earth deposits in Kachin State. “Among the proposals,” it reported, “are one advocating talks with Myanmar’s ruling junta to get a peace deal with the Kachin Independence Army rebels and another calling for the U.S. to instead work directly with the KIA without engaging the junta.”
Among those advancing these proposals was none other than Adam Castillo, who was present during a July 17 meeting at Vice President J.D. Vance’s office in Washington.
It is hard to know how far things will proceed from here. The Reuters report makes clear that Vance “has also met in person and virtually with the democratic opposition and ethnic armed groups fighting the military,” and the State Department told the news agency that its engagement with the Min Aung Hlaing administration “does not diminish its relationships with other groups.”
Any step toward further re-engagement with Naypyidaw, let alone a dropping of U.S. sanctions against Min Aung Hlaing and other senior officials, is likely to prompt strong criticism. While the new quasi-civilian government has attempted to project an image of control and normalcy, the political situation in the country remains febrile. The post-coup civil war, which continues despite the inauguration of the new government, has now killed more than 100,000 people and displaced 3.8 million more. In a report released yesterday, the U.N. Development Programme stated that more than two in three people in Myanmar are now in “multidimensional poverty” or are at risk of falling into it, due to the “simultaneous collapse” of the healthcare and education systems, and the atrophying of the economy.
Since taking office as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has embarked on a diplomatic charm offensive aimed at consolidating key partnerships and normalizing Naypyidaw’s relationship with key partners, including the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Indeed, the former general has just departed from Malaysia, where, in another notable policy reversal, he was accorded full state honors by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. He has also visited Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, and Thailand in recent months, in pursuit of Myanmar’s full reintegration into the 11-nation bloc.
Re-engagement with the U.S., even to a limited degree, would be another diplomatic victory for Min Aung Hlaing. Whether this would end up yielding benefits for the U.S., however, remains unclear. In his article for CFR, Kurlantzick argued that the U.S. succesfully gaining access to Myanmar’s rare earths “is hard to imagine,” given their proximity to the Chinese border and their location in regions “where Beijing wields dominant influence.”
Beyond this, Kurlantzick argued, “Engaging with the regime now will simply show powerful autocrats that their collaboration works, and democracies accede. And it will cause more misery for the citizens of one of the most benighted places in the world.”

articles.title: What ‘Beyond Advocacy’ Means for India’s Role in the Russia-Ukraine Conflict
articles.full_text:
India’s possible role as a facilitator will be driven by its own economic interests, rather than any need to increase its political heft on the global stage.
India’s Foreign Minister S Jaishankar shakes hands with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha at their meeting in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 3, 2026.
Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting earlier this week, India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar said that India’s consistent position that the Russia-Ukraine conflict should end through “dialogue and diplomacy” between the concerned parties remains unchanged. In the same breath, he acknowledged that New Delhi in “recent months” has been a “little more involved beyond advocacy” in negotiating an end to the conflict.
Without providing details, the Indian foreign minister said India was engaged in discussions with both sides on specific arrangements involving Black Sea shipping, grain and energy exports, and possible “non-attack” understandings. During the latest press briefing, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs confirmed that New Delhi was having “ongoing conversations with both Russia and Ukraine” on these matters.
Earlier, in his address at the United Nations General Assembly, Jaishankar said that New Delhi was “prepared to do everything possible” to ameliorate the conflict in Ukraine, “especially with regard to food and energy security.”
As part of this activism to broker peace and operational agreements, New Delhi, along with the United States, Egypt, and Turkiye, reportedly submitted a proposal for a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, which Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described as the “most extensive.” That proposal followed Jaishankar’s visit to Kyiv on September 3, the first-ever standalone bilateral visit by an Indian foreign minister to Ukraine.
According to a press release from the Embassy of Ukraine in India, the discussions between Jaishankar and Sybiha focused on the situation in the Black Sea and freedom of navigation, global food security, nuclear threats posed by Russia, and the development of India-Ukraine relations.
Indian media reports cited unnamed government sources to confirm that a truce plan was discussed during Jaishankar’s visit to Kyiv.
Despite moving beyond rhetorical calls for dialogue toward concrete proposal-based diplomacy, New Delhi has not formally described its role as a mediator. Its reticence probably stems from its own antipathy toward mediation when it comes to its disputes with Pakistan on the Kashmir issue. Referring to Pakistan’s mediation efforts in the ongoing war in West Asia, Jaishankar commented that India would not be a “dalal (broker)” nation like Islamabad.
New Delhi has strong relations with Russia. It would, therefore, not want to jeopardize ties with its trusted partner by taking any position that could go against President Vladimir Putin’s domestic interests, especially. This is why, despite repeated criticism from the West for its perceived “pro-Russia” position, New Delhi has refrained from publicly censuring Russian actions in Ukraine and voted against or abstained on most Ukraine-related resolutions at the United Nations.
So far, Moscow has responded positively to New Delhi’s peace efforts, with Putin publicly praising Prime Minister Narendra Modi for his “ideas and persistent efforts” for peace in the ongoing war in Ukraine. During his talks with Putin on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek earlier this year, Modi urged the Russian leader to move from “endless war” to the “end of war” for the sake of humanity.
Nevertheless, the shift in New Delhi’s tone, small as it is at present, is an important development. It reflects domestic concerns over the war’s economic costs on India.
Both Russia and Ukraine are major suppliers of several essential commodities to India, including agricultural products. Supply chain disruptions caused by the conflict have already had a major impact on the Indian economy. A notable example is the extraordinary surge in the price of sunflower oil, which Russia and Ukraine supply to India. Due to supply chain disruptions caused by attacks on cargo ships in the Black Sea, New Delhi’s sunflower oil imports fell to their lowest level in more than four years in September. Consequently, between October 2025 and October 2026, retail prices increased by 18.7 percent.
Beyond economic motives, humanitarian concerns also drive New Delhi’s position. Targeted strikes on commercial shipping in the Black Sea continue to claim the lives of Indian seafarers, who account for the second largest share of the global maritime workforce.
Additionally, Indian businesses have faced severe financial losses due to the recent escalation in the conflict. In August, a Russian airstrike targeted a site at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, owned by Indian businessman Lakshmi Mittal, forcing a partial shutdown of the plant. More recently, on October 4, Russian attacks heavily damaged the Indian-owned Kusum Healthcare pharmaceutical plant, resulting in estimated losses of $50 million.
New Delhi’s more robust approach toward negotiating an end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict is also being appreciated by its European partners. Previously, India’s “cautious” position on the Ukraine crisis has caused some friction in the EU-India relationship. As New Delhi’s traditional partnership with Washington encounters friction, strengthening alignments with partners in Europe is increasingly becoming a strategic necessity.
Going forward, New Delhi is unlikely to mediate directly between Russia and Ukraine, given the complexity and historical baggage of the conflict. More likely, it will play a more important, visible political and diplomatic role, acting as a facilitator of dialogue. This role will be determined by India’s own economic interests, likely to focus on issue-based negotiations, rather than to increase its political heft on the global stage by acting as direct mediator.

articles.title: One Year On, China’s K Visa Remains an Opaque Promise
articles.full_text:
China’s flagship talent visa can be found in the official application system, but most of the specifics on who can apply, and how to do so, are still missing.
In September 2026, a British physicist posted an update to a months-long Reddit thread, writing that he finally had a K visa and that the visa “does exist.” The process had taken roughly five months from application to passport collection, although he acknowledged that part of the delay was his own doing, since one of his degree certificates had to be reissued and an embassy email sat unnoticed in his spam folder. 
The application itself, as he described it, was simple; there was no interview, no invitation letter, and no question about his plans in China, and he found the visa center staff patient and helpful. The visa he received is valid for ten years, permits multiple entries, and allows stays of 180 days.
What made his post notable was its rarity. His is one of the few first-person accounts I found of a successful K visa application online. That is why applicants from Pakistan to the United States had followed his thread for months, asking for updates on his application and comparing their own experiences in the absence of detailed official guidance.
China’s Foreign Ministry’s own online application guide shows why that guidance is needed. For São Paulo, the submission city I examined, the guide lists the K visa among the available categories and allows applicants to identify themselves as graduates of well-known universities or as employees of well-known research institutions. Although the category is therefore visible, the page neither explains how “well-known” is assessed nor displays a checklist of supporting documents specific to the K visa. As a result, applicants can find the category but cannot determine from the online guidance whether they meet its requirements or what evidence they should submit.
The K visa exists, and there are public accounts of successful applications. What applicants cannot obtain from the sources I reviewed is the information needed to assess their own prospects. There is also no public indication of scale, since China has not published how many K visas it has issued.

The domestic reception was far less welcoming. In the days before the launch, hashtags about the K visa drew tens of millions of views on Weibo, where the policy arrived at a difficult moment. Urban youth unemployment stood near 19 percent, and recirculated clips of Indian media celebrating the visa persuaded many commenters that foreign competitors were about to enter China’s already strained job market. On September 30, the state-run People’s Daily responded with a commentary titled “Distorting the K visa will only mislead the public,” which rebutted the criticisms one by one and promised that the new visa would come with “supporting management systems.”
Those supporting systems have not been published in the year since. In January, University World News reported that four government agencies were still jointly drafting implementation guidelines, which were expected to specify university rankings, subject lists, and age limits. Applications were expected to open by April 2026 at the earliest. 
April passed without an announcement. In May immigration practitioners noted that the parameters for the K visa – including the age range defining “young,” the standard for “well-known” universities, document checklists, and fees – remained unpublished. As of early October, the public guidance I have reviewed still does not resolve these questions.
A comparison with China’s other openings is instructive. China has expanded visa-free access; such entries rose 49.5 percent in 2025. More directly related to the K visa, Shanghai’s Lingang new area published new measures designed to facilitate foreign talent residence in 2026. For both visa-free access and the Lingang new area measures, the guidance clearly states who qualifies and on what terms. 
The K visa, by contrast, specifies the related fields and its minimum degree requirement, while the age boundary defining “young,” the standard for “well-known” universities, and the evidence required remain unstated. Applicants cannot determine whether they meet the requirement or how to demonstrate that they do.
In the vacuum, the standards that applicants encounter depend on the office they approach. An applicant in Pakistan reported that, after a month of waiting, the embassy told him the K visa “hasn’t been rolled out yet” in his region, and that the local document portal demanded a master’s degree although official explanatory guidance specifies a bachelor’s degree. Another applicant recounted being told in Beijing that the visa was reserved for fresh 2025 graduates, a criterion that doesn’t appear in any public document. The British physicist, by contrast, was approved in London as a Ph.D. holder who had graduated several years earlier, facing no such constraints. 
These accounts are self-reported and should be read with caution. The difficulty is that, one year in, such self-reports are the only available accounts of how K visa applications are handled, because no official source settles these questions. When terms such as “well-known universities” remain undefined, applicants cannot assess their eligibility in advance, while the interpretation of these requirements remains with the officials reviewing their applications.
It’s not clear why the implementation guidelines have not appeared. Practitioners and scholars have offered technical explanations. Shi Hui, a senior partner at the law firm Dacheng, attributed the delay to the need for government departments to finalize supporting operational details, update the visa application and review system, and coordinate processes across agencies. Liu Guofu of the Beijing Institute of Technology, a leading scholar of Chinese immigration law, identified system upgrades and the establishment of procedures for an “employer-independent” visa, a category new to China’s immigration framework, as the primary technical challenge. 
There is precedent for such a gradual path. The R visa for high-level foreign talent was created in 2013 and was supplemented in 2017 by implementation measures that further specified its conditions and procedures. These measures were extended nationwide in 2018 after trials in nine provinces and cities. That means the R visa took five years to go from the initial announcement to national application.
There may be a political explanation for the delay as well. The backlash to the K visa’s launch plausibly raised the political cost of visible implementation. The absence of published guidelines – and especially the lack of hard counts of the number of visas being issued – is consistent with that reading as well as theories about administrative difficulty. 
Chinese officials justified the K visa by pointing to global talent competition; in its editorial, People’s Daily cited a projected shortfall of nearly 30 million workers in key manufacturing fields. However, critics evaluate the K visa against domestic youth unemployment, which reached 18.9 percent again in August 2026, its highest level in a year. These are two different standards for judging what openness is for.
The reaction among the visa’s supposed beneficiaries suggests a parallel misalignment. In one thread on an Indian diaspora forum – admittedly a single discussion rather than a representative survey – the top-voted response to a question about the K visa held that “Chinese government want K Visa folks but Chinese people won’t want K Visa folks.” Another commenter wrote, “I might consider a BYD car in India sooner than I’d consider a second innings as an NRI [Non-Resident Indian, an Indian citizen living abroad] in China.” The reasons offered – including language, “996” work culture, geopolitics, and China’s own youth unemployment – mirror the anxieties voiced on the Chinese side. 
Such threads suggest that both the feared influx of foreign workers and the promised talent wave may be overstated. Each public is responding to domestic concerns at least as much as to the policy itself.
The K visa thus merits continued observation. Upon its launch, the visa was widely read as China’s entry into an intensifying global competition for scientific and technological talent. Its opaque beginning shows how much administrative work it takes to go from declaring an opening to building a channel that qualified foreigners can actually use. Whether the coming year brings published criteria, issuance figures, and consistent consular practice will indicate how far China intends to pursue that competition in practice as well as in announcement. This makes the K visa a case worth following for anyone watching how the global contest over STEM talent unfolds.
In September 2026, a British physicist posted an update to a months-long Reddit thread, writing that he finally had a K visa and that the visa “does exist.” The process had taken roughly five months from application to passport collection, although he acknowledged that part of the delay was his own doing, since one of his degree certificates had to be reissued and an embassy email sat unnoticed in his spam folder. 
The application itself, as he described it, was simple; there was no interview, no invitation letter, and no question about his plans in China, and he found the visa center staff patient and helpful. The visa he received is valid for ten years, permits multiple entries, and allows stays of 180 days.
What made his post notable was its rarity. His is one of the few first-person accounts I found of a successful K visa application online. That is why applicants from Pakistan to the United States had followed his thread for months, asking for updates on his application and comparing their own experiences in the absence of detailed official guidance.
China’s Foreign Ministry’s own online application guide shows why that guidance is needed. For São Paulo, the submission city I examined, the guide lists the K visa among the available categories and allows applicants to identify themselves as graduates of well-known universities or as employees of well-known research institutions. Although the category is therefore visible, the page neither explains how “well-known” is assessed nor displays a checklist of supporting documents specific to the K visa. articles.title: The Afghan Taliban’s Growing Drone War Against Pakistan
articles.full_text:
For Pakistan, the most worrying possibility is small, relatively cheap drone systems falling into the hands of terrorist groups.
Pakistan’s air defense system shot down eight drones after they entered the country’s airspace from Afghanistan on September 23. Four drones were shot down near the border at Torkham and four were shot down near Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In response, Pakistan struck 10 locations in Afghanistan that were being used to launch and store drones by the Afghan Taliban.
This growing use of drones has added a dangerous new dimension to an already fragile Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship. On its western border, Pakistan now faces a two-pronged security challenge: first, the direct use of drones by the Afghan Taliban against Pakistani security positions and other targets, and second, the transfer or facilitation of drone technology to affiliated militant groups such as the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), enabling them to conduct attacks against military check posts and other targets inside Pakistan. What was once primarily a tool of surveillance, propaganda, and battlefield observation has evolved into an instrument capable of extending the reach, precision, and lethality of militant violence. 
The Afghan Taliban began using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in 2016, initially for propaganda purposes. Over time, however, their use expanded into operational roles, including reconnaissance, surveillance, and the delivery of explosives. Between February 27 to March 15, 2026 the Afghan Taliban claimed responsibility for 15 drone attacks in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province and Islamabad. 
The Afghan Taliban procures its drones from a mix of sources, including commercially available platforms, systems obtained through regional networks, and locally modified or assembled equipment. This has made drone technology more accessible and harder to control. 
The Afghan Taliban’s 313th Battalion, associated with the Haqqani network, is using one-way attack drones, referred to as kamikaze drones. The Afghan Taliban drones are launched from Kandahar, Nangarhar, Paktia, and Paktika, reducing the distance to targets in Quetta, Peshawar, Islamabad, and Waziristan in Pakistan. Recently, the Afghan Taliban have reportedly acquired anti-drone systems and are preparing to deploy them at the 205th Corps in Kandahar and near Spin Boldak to counter Pakistani drones along the border.
The concern becomes more acute when this capability is viewed alongside the TTP and other militant groups operating from Afghanistan into Pakistan. These groups have shown considerable adaptability in adopting new technologies, especially drones. This low-cost technology gives militant groups capabilities once associated primarily with conventional military forces. For Pakistan, the challenge is therefore not simply the presence of drones, but the growing ease with which this technology can be acquired, adapted and deployed by multiple actors across the border.
Pakistan has so far effectively intercepted cross-border drone incursions from Afghanistan. However, it needs to take further concrete steps, as drone use is becoming a persistent feature of the Afghan Taliban’s military strategy against Pakistan. 
The most worrying possibility is not necessarily that Afghanistan will develop a large drone fleet. It is the multiplication of small, relatively cheap systems. A conventional military platform represents a significant investment and is therefore used selectively. Small unmanned systems can be acquired in larger numbers and employed repeatedly. They can observe a security position, identify a target, test air defense responses, and also carry an explosive payload. Even when they cause limited physical damage, they can create disruption, fear, and uncertainty. Pakistan therefore needs to treat counter-drone capability as a central component of national security rather than as a specialized military requirement.
There has already been movement toward domestic drone production. Pakistan’s defense industry and armed forces have experience with UAVs for surveillance, reconnaissance, and combat roles. Indigenous production is important because reliance on foreign suppliers can become a vulnerability during a prolonged crisis. A country facing an evolving drone threat needs the ability not only to build systems but also to modify, repair, and upgrade them according to its own requirements.
Pakistan also requires a layered counter-UAV architecture. The first layer should be detection. Conventional radar does not always provide an adequate answer against small, low-flying drones, particularly in cluttered urban or mountainous regions like Pakistan’s western tribal borderlands. Pakistan therefore needs a combination of short-range radar, electro-optical and infrared sensors, radio-frequency detection, and other technologies capable of identifying unusual aerial activity. 
The second layer is neutralization. Depending on the threat, this could involve electronic warfare, communications jamming, spoofing, and conventional interceptors. No single technology is likely to be effective against every type of drone. A layered approach is therefore essential for Pakistan to counter the layered threat. 
Pakistan should also invest in artificial intelligence and data analysis. A modern counter-drone system should learn from repeated attacks: launch patterns, flight routes, frequencies, operating times, and target selection. The objective should be to move from reacting to drones after detection toward predicting likely attacks before they occur. Therefore, working in this direction should be a priority of Islamabad. 
Airports, power stations, military facilities, government buildings, oil installations, and major communication centers all require appropriate protection. Border management must consequently become more technologically sophisticated. Pakistan’s long and difficult western border cannot be secured through conventional fencing and physical posts alone. Sensors, surveillance aircraft, drones, ground-based monitoring systems, and rapid-response units need to operate as one network. Intelligence sharing between civilian and military agencies is equally important.
At the same time, Islamabad must avoid allowing the drone issue to become part of a permanent cycle of escalation with Kabul. Retaliatory action may be presented as necessary when attacks occur, but military responses alone cannot produce a stable border. Each strike carries the possibility of further retaliation, civilian casualties, and a broader deterioration in relations.
The Afghan Taliban therefore needs to come to the negotiating table. Dialogue does not require Pakistan to abandon its security concerns or accept attacks against its territory. On the contrary, negotiations should be used to establish verifiable commitments by the Afghan Taliban: Afghan territory must not be used for attacks against Pakistan; militants should not receive access to military technology in Afghanistan; mechanisms for investigating cross-border incidents should be created; and both sides should maintain direct communication during crises.

articles.title: Investigation Finds That Former High-Ranking Uzbek Security Official Acquired UAE Citizenship
articles.full_text:
According to an OCCRP and Ozodlik investigation, Otabek Umarov, the Uzbek president’s son-in-law, obtained Emirati citizenship in 2023, while he was deputy head of the Presidential Security Service.
In April 2023, when he was serving as deputy head of the Presidential Security Service, Otabek Umarov – Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s son-in-law – reportedly acquired citizenship in the United Arab Emirates. He’s also alleged to be the owner of around $7 million worth of Dubai real estate.
Those are the central allegations of a new investigation published by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) and RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service, Ozodlik.
Under Uzbek military law, which governs the position Umarov held at the time, holding a second citizenship is prohibited. Since acquiring citizenship typically includes swearing an oath of allegiance, many countries bar security (and other) officials from doing so – a second passport represents possible divided loyalties and a counterintelligence risk.
As OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and [the process] requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.”
Umarov was shifted out of his security service role in November 2024, in the extended wake of the assassination attempt on Komil Allamjanov. 
Allamjanov, at the time of the October 2024 attempt, had recently stepped down from his role as deputy head of the presidential administration. He has since returned to government service, as an adviser to the powerful head of the presidential administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva (the president’s eldest daughter). As of January 2026 he was also appointed to a seemingly bespoke role: advisor-ambassador and representative of the presidential administration in the United States.
Umarov, meanwhile, was named first deputy chairman of Uzbekistan’s National Olympic Committee – his father-in-law, the president, is the chairman.
According to OCCRP and Ozodlik, at some point in 2025, Umarov became the owner of 13 properties in Dubai, worth around $7 million. The properties previously belonged to his younger brother, Oybek Umarov, who purchased them in 2021 and 2022, according to leaked Dubai real estate data obtained by OCCRP. 
It is not clear precisely how or when they came to be listed with Umarov’s name on the deeds, whether the properties were gifted or purchased. 
While Umarov has notably expensive tastes – for example, he’s been pictured wearing a limited edition Richard Mille watch valued at up to $1.9 million – his government position doesn’t quite explain his apparent wealth. Uzbek officials do not have to disclose their income declarations publicly.
OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Public commercial registries show no record of [Otabek Umarov] owning private companies during his time as deputy presidential security chief.” His brother, however, does have extensive business holdings, including in banking, cement, and metalwork. 
A high-ranking government source told The Diplomat in late 2024 that Umarov’s assets and businesses were held in the names of others, including Ulugbek Shadmanov who was implicated in an apparent attempt to manipulate the U.S. sanctions system to target Allamjonov and another Uzbek official in the months before the assassination attempt. Shadmanov was earlier named in the Pandora Papers as connected to an offshore company, though there are few details available. In December 2024 he was detained in Dubai and extradited rapidly – apparently without the proper legal process – to Uzbekistan, regardless of the fact that he held what’s known as a “Golden Visa” in the UAE. Despite high-powered legal representation and a campaign on his behalf, very little has been reported since about his case. 
Ultimately, the OCCRP and Ozodlik investigation raises far more questions than it answers; that’s the nature of investigations into the opaque underbelly of Uzbek politics (and those of the UAE, to boot). As I told Ozodlik, we don’t know exactly how Umarov acquired UAE citizenship, who was involved, and who knew about it. As noted above, the process to acquired UAE citizenship necessitates a nomination by a royal court or senior official. It’s nearly impossible to believe that Umarov’s role and connections were unknown at the time to the UAE’s authorities.
Then there are questions of what comes next. Uzbekistan does not officially recognize dual citizenship. Holding a second citizenship isn’t illegal per se – though it does violate laws related to Umarov’s specific position at the time. Nevertheless, “voluntarily acquiring a passport of a foreign state” is listed as possible grounds for revocation of Uzbek citizenship.

articles.title: Beyond Deference: India’s Bangladesh Reckoning
articles.full_text:
A course correction is needed in New Delhi.
On October 6, Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi called on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi. It isn’t unusual for heads of Indian missions assigned to critical or sensitive bilateral stations to provide direct update or receive specific strategic directives during visits or consultations in New Delhi. Modi’s office maintains an active and hands-on approach to foreign policy implementation, making direct communication and briefings with key diplomatic personnel a standard part of administrative routine. However, Trivedi’s case and the circumstances of the meeting are rather unique. 
Trivedi was appointed as India’s high commissioner to Bangladesh in April 2026, a rare political appointment to a key neighboring diplomatic mission. A businessman and a politician of the ruling BJP from the eastern state of West Bengal, he has direct access to Modi and does not need to route his meetings through the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). His appointment to Dhaka in April 2026, replacing a career diplomat, came at a time when bilateral relations between India and Bangladesh had hit a rough patch. 
Bangladeshi demands for the deportation of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has found refuge in India since August 2024, has been a particular sore point. India has ignored repeated pleas by the new BNP government and its predecessor interim government to extradite Hasina, despite the existence of an extradition treaty between the two countries since 2013. The treaty’s terms (Article 6) allows either country to refuse extradition if the offense is of a political nature. 
Three days before his meeting with Modi, Trivedi’s response to a direct question at the Bay of Bengal Conversation (BoBC) 2026 in Dhaka had hit the headlines. The BoBC is an annual international conference with participants from over a hundred countries comprising world leaders, policymakers, diplomats, researchers, academics, experts, and civil society representatives organized by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS). I participated in the conference, held this year on October 3-4, as a panelist and a guest of the CGS. 
A participating Bangladeshi student asked the Indian high commissioner: “When will India send back Hasina?” Trivedi appeared to diplomatically avert the direct query and instead passed the buck to the Bangladeshi military, who had sent her to India on a military aircraft before she even resigned from her post. Moreover, Hasina was meant to be transiting via Delhi to a third country, which never actually materialized. This put New Delhi in a quandary.
“At that point in time, she [Hasina] was still the prime minister of Bangladesh. We had hardly any choice on that. It was our duty as a neighbor to accept the reality of life,” Trivedi said. While no press statements were issued, the meeting between Modi and Trivedi may reflect an effort on New Delhi’s part to gauge Dhaka’s mood from its own representative. New Delhi still envisages that a visit by the Bangladeshi prime minister to India could create opportunities for an exchange of views and break fresh ground in normalizing relations, but it has yet to embark upon a path that will create the enabling environment necessary for such movement. To the contrary, India’s actions have not inspired much confidence in Bangladesh. 
First, from time to time India has allowed Sheikh Hasina to issue press statements denouncing the BNP government, despite Dhaka’s objections. Second, India continues to forcibly deport “illegal Bangladeshi migrants.” A large part of the process involves physically pushing these people under the cover of darkness into Bangladeshi territory while ignoring Dhaka’s objections to such a practice. Fifth, even two months after Dhaka informed Delhi of its choice for its next ambassador to India, India hasn’t approved the posting. This can be seen as a pressure tactic at its very best. 
The irony is that, to New Delhi’s discomfiture, Dhaka is carving out a new framework to deal with India. articles.title: Afghanistan and the BLA’s Evolving Capabilities
articles.full_text:
Reported discussions in Kandahar point to a possible expansion of the BLA’s external support networks as the group comes under pressure in Pakistan.
On October 1, Pakistan’s military said that representatives of several militant groups had met in Kandahar in August to discuss coordinating manpower and operations against Pakistani security forces. Military spokesperson Lt. Gen. Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry said the meeting was chaired by Mullah Shirleen, the Taliban-appointed governor of Kandahar, and involved representatives of the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) seeking additional fighters from networks associated with Hafiz Gul Bahadur, a Pakistani militant leader based in North Waziristan. A separate intelligence report identified figures linked to al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS) among those present. 
For the BLA, the significance of the meeting lies less in the presence of other militant groups than in what access to Afghanistan could provide the organization: additional manpower, relationships with established militant networks, and a deeper operating environment beyond Balochistan. The reported discussions therefore point to a possible expansion of the BLA’s external support networks at a time when the group has been developing more sophisticated operational capabilities. 
Afghan officials denied that the meeting took place, and the allegations have not been independently established. Pakistan has long accused the Taliban government of sheltering militants, and relations between the two countries are openly hostile. Fighting in October 2025 killed dozens and nearly closed the border; cross-border strikes resumed in February 2026 and continued intermittently through September. Each side’s claims therefore deserve caution. But we can still consider the basic question: what role is Afghanistan playing in the BLA’s evolving military capabilities? 
A United Nations Security Council monitoring report published in August found that BLA members had access to U.S.- and NATO-origin equipment left behind in Afghanistan, including M4 and M16 rifles, reconnaissance drones, night-vision devices, and thermal equipment. The report also cited information from a member state that BLA members had trained alongside Tehreek-e-Taliban (TTP) personnel at facilities in Afghanistan, including in drone and urban warfare.
The BLA’s January 2026 offensive illustrated these capabilities being put to use in its operations. On January 31, the group claimed simultaneous attacks across Balochistan, including Quetta, Gwadar, Noshki and Panjgur. Pakistan’s military said 18 civilians and 15 security personnel died and that its forces killed 92 militants, while the BLA said it killed 84 security personnel. Neither tally has been independently confirmed. 
A February assessment reported that the group had used drones, satellite communications, and U.S.-made weapons, linking some of the weaponry to equipment left behind in Afghanistan. That does not mean every drone or rifle came from there, however, since commercial drones, communications equipment, and weapons can be obtained through multiple channels. 
One such channel is Balochistan’s western border with Iran. BLA and Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) members have reportedly maintained a presence in Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan province, and in January 2024 Pakistan struck locations there that it identified as belonging to the two groups. The BLF denied having hideouts there, and there is no established evidence that Iran supplies the BLA with weapons. Afghanistan is different, because the U.N. report documents both equipment access and training. 
The BLA’s outreach to Kandahar may also reflect pressure rather than strength. The Associated Press, which saw the intelligence report, paraphrased the document as saying that “BLA representatives told participants that Pakistani military operations had left the group short of fighters and resources.” According to the report, Afghan intelligence officials responded by assuring the BLA that militants with the TTP and AQIS could provide manpower, weapons, and logistical support for operations in Balochistan. 
The same report alleged that Afghan and Indian intelligence officials helped arrange the meeting. India has consistently denied backing the BLA, so that claim also warrants scrutiny. Taken together, however, the reported discussions suggest that the BLA may be looking to Afghanistan not simply as a sanctuary, but as a source of personnel, equipment, and connections that could help offset pressure from Pakistani military operations. 
Meanwhile, Pakistan has escalated its response to the Taliban’s support for militant groups. Hours before the army’s briefing, Pakistan said it had carried out airstrikes in Helmand and Kunar provinces, while on September 24 it reported strikes on 10 locations in Kandahar, Paktia, and Khost. Such airstrikes may disrupt specific sites, but they do not by themselves cut the flow of weapons, training and recruits.
Three indicators will help clarify the extent of Afghanistan’s support for the BLA: independent verification of the Kandahar meeting, further U.N. monitoring of equipment and training links, and whether the group’s use of drones and coordinated assaults expands beyond the scale documented in earlier operations. The evidence of BLA access to equipment and networks in Afghanistan is significant. What remains unproven is how much of the group’s growing operational sophistication can be attributed to that access.
For Pakistan, the way forward is to address the BLA threat without reducing the wider Balochistan issue to a security response alone. Preventing militant groups from using Afghanistan as a source of recruits, training, and equipment will require continued engagement with Afghan authorities, particularly over the TTP and other groups operating from Afghan territory. 
At the same time, greater attention to the security, economic and political concerns of Baloch communities can help separate the grievances of local populations from the armed groups seeking to exploit them. A combination of diplomacy with Kabul, stronger border coordination, and targeted counterterrorism measures, alongside greater engagement with communities in Balochistan, would give Pakistan a more sustainable way to contain cross-border militant networks while reducing the risk of further regional escalation.
